summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: 'Do not eat' warning issued to Tesco shoppers after 'health risk' recall
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Tesco is warning shoppers not to eat one of its products which has been recalled due to a potential health risk. The supermarket giant is recalling the Tesco Finest Caesar & Smoked Bacon Coleslaw due to a packaging error. The mistake means that some packs may actually contain Tesco Finest Four Cheese Potato Salad, meaning that it also contains mustard not declared on the label. As a result, it is a possible health hazard for anyone with an allergy to mustard. Wednesday 3rd September - Tesco recalls Tesco Finest Caesar & Smoked Bacon Coleslaw because of undeclared mustard #FoodAllergy https://t.co/JRHL6RKA7q pic.twitter.com/YU0gMmSKs2 — Food Standards Agency (@foodgov) September 3, 2026 The affected coleslaw comes in 270g packets and has a use by date of September 4. A spokesman for the Food Standards Agency said: “Tesco is recalling the above product from customers and has contacted the relevant allergy support organisations, which will tell their members about the recall. “The company has also issued a recall notice to its customers. These notices explain to customers why the product is being recalled and tell them what to do if they have bought the product. “If you have bought the above product and have an allergy to mustard do not eat it. Instead return it to any Tesco store for a full refund. “For further details, please visit the contact page of Tesco's website: tesco.com/help/contact.” Tesco added: “If you’ve bought the affected product and have an allergy to mustard, please don’t eat. “Instead, return the product to any Tesco store where a full refund will be given. No receipt is required. “No other Tesco products are affected by this recall. We’re sorry for any inconvenience caused.” If there is a problem with a food product that means it should not be sold, then it might be 'withdrawn' (taken off the shelves) or 'recalled' (when customers are asked to return the product). The FSA issues Product Withdrawal Information Notices and Product Recall Information Notices to let consumers and local authorities know about problems associated with food. In some cases, a 'Food Alert for Action' is issued. This provides local authorities with details of specific actions to be taken on behalf of consumers.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: State Pension age rises to 67 - who will be hit hardest as age goes up?
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Millions of people are facing a longer wait for their State Pension, but some could be hit much harder than others. The State Pension age is rising from 66 to 67, with the change being phased in between April 2026 and April 2028. For someone who is healthy and able to remain in work, waiting longer may be manageable. But for others, those extra months could create a serious financial gap, particularly if they have little savings and are unable to continue working. A tax expert has warned that seven groups could be particularly vulnerable as the new State Pension age takes effect. The Work and Pensions Committee has previously warned that the impact of the increase is unlikely to be felt equally across the country. Andy Wood, a tax expert at Tax Barrister UK, said: “The increase means that affected individuals will have to wait longer before becoming eligible for their State Pension. “For those who are healthy, in secure employment and able to continue working, that additional wait may be manageable. "However, it could create a serious financial gap for people who cannot remain in work and do not have sufficient savings or other assets to support themselves.” The groups identified as particularly vulnerable include: These circumstances can overlap, potentially leaving some people facing several financial pressures at once. Someone who has spent years in a physically demanding, lower-paid job, for example, may also have caring responsibilities or health problems that make it difficult to work until their new State Pension age. Wood said: “These circumstances frequently overlap. Someone may have worked in a lower-paid or physically demanding job while also having caring responsibilities or experiencing health problems. “This can make it more difficult to build private pension savings, accumulate other assets or continue working until the new State Pension age. “People approaching retirement should therefore check their expected State Pension age and forecast rather than assuming they will automatically become eligible when they turn 66.” Recommended reading: The rise from 66 to 67 is not happening overnight. It is being introduced gradually, meaning the exact date someone becomes eligible depends on their date of birth. People born between 6 April 1960 and 5 March 1961 will reach State Pension age at 66 plus a specified number of months. For example, someone born on 31 July 1960 is expected to reach State Pension age at 66 years and four months. This means people approaching retirement should not simply assume that turning 66 means their State Pension will start. Wood said: “The exact date on which someone becomes eligible will depend on their date of birth. It is important to check this directly through the Government’s State Pension age service, particularly when making retirement or employment plans. “People should also check their National Insurance record and State Pension forecast. Reaching State Pension age does not necessarily mean everyone will receive the same amount, as entitlement will depend on an individual’s National Insurance history.” For someone unable to continue working, the wait for their State Pension could mean relying on other sources of income for longer. That could include working-age benefits or savings that had originally been earmarked for retirement. The Work and Pensions Committee has highlighted concerns about the potential impact on people who cannot remain in employment until their State Pension age. Previous evidence also indicated that when the State Pension age increased from 65 to 66, the absolute poverty rate among 65-year-olds more than doubled. Wood said: “A delay of several months may sound relatively small, but it could represent a considerable loss of expected income for someone who has already left work. “Those without substantial savings may need to rely on Universal Credit or other available support until they qualify for their State Pension. Others could be forced to use retirement savings earlier than planned. “The change may be particularly difficult for people in physically demanding roles or those with medical conditions that limit the type or amount of work they can undertake.” The committee has called on the Government to consider increasing Universal Credit payments for 66-year-olds affected by the transition. The changes do not stop at 67. Under current legislation, the State Pension age is due to rise again from 67 to 68 between 2044 and 2046. However, that timetable could still change following future Government reviews. For anyone approaching retirement, the key point is that their State Pension age is determined by their date of birth, rather than simply reaching their 66th birthday. Checking the Government's State Pension age service, National Insurance record and State Pension forecast could help people understand when they are likely to qualify and how much they may receive. For those unable to continue working and without significant savings, knowing the date in advance could be particularly important when planning how to bridge the gap before State Pension payments begin.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Rare warbird forced to make a belly landing after engine issue
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A rare warbird was forced to make a belly landing after suffering an engine issue during a maintenance check flight. The Fighter Collection's Curtiss P-40C Warhawk G-CIIO came down northwest of Royston on August 25 after taking off from IWM Duxford, in Cambridgeshire. The aircraft suffered an engine issue during a maintenance check flight which forced the pilot to perform a wheels up landing. The pilot evacuated unaided and directed the Duxford Fire & Rescue Team to the scene. The Fighter Collection said: "We are indebted to the IWM security team for providing mobile security units to the site ensuring the safety of the aircraft whilst the engineering team dismantled the aircraft." Highfield Farm staff helped lift the aircraft on to its landing gear before it was towed to safety. The Fighter Collection added: "We are further indebted to the Welch's Specialist Movements team who provided the logistics and highways permits to repatriate the airframe back to hangar T2S today." The Curtiss P-40C Warhawk served with several Allied air forces during the Second World War and was America’s third most-produced fighter of the conflict. The aircraft is rare in the UK, with G-CIIO one of only three airworthy examples before last week’s incident.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Miniature railway plans submitted for Huntingdonshire community nursery site
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Find, save and share Public Notices that affect you in the  area. The Public Notice Portal carries statutory public notices published in local newspapers and is the fastest and most effective way of finding out what is happening in YOUR neighbourhood. A planning application has been lodged for a miniature railway at a Godmanchester Community Nursery after council enforcement officers halted work the project. The plan would put the railway along the eastern and northern edges of the five-acre, volunteer-run Godmanchester Community Plant Nursery on Park Lane, which includes a community orchard, with the aim of adding an attraction for families. A design, access, and heritage statement submitted alongside the application says work had begun on the railway track base before Huntingdonshire District Council enforcement officers stopped it, and the application seeks permission for the work already done and to finish the railway. Harry Quenault submitted the scheme for Godmanchester Town Council, with planning agent Chris McCrae acting for the applicant; the application describes it as the "installation of a miniature railway". Eye level image of the existing track installation adjacent to the southern 'platform 1', demonstrating its low impact on the land. (Image: Godmanchester Community Plant Nursery) The statement says the railway would attract visitors while keeping rides affordable at £1, and supporters say it would offer families a cheap activity, encourage repeat visits and improve access to the site’s rare apple orchard. The design and heritage statement says the railway would complement, not replace, the nursery’s role as a community resource. It states: "The proposal is not to turn the site into a theme park. It is to add a modest attraction that complements horticulture, outdoor activity and community access." The document also points to Godmanchester’s railway heritage through the former Huntingdon to St Ives line, and planners say the attraction could introduce younger generations to the area’s railway history and draw more visitors. Eye level image traveling toward the northern end of the site, illustrating the track base prepared to receive the track prior to enforcement notice. (Image: Godmanchester Community Plant Nursery) The railway would run mostly at ground level, with two platforms, a turntable at the northern end and a low timber fence around the track, and planning documents say the route is designed to minimise its impact on the orchard and neighbouring properties. The site is in a flood-risk area, but the applicant says the project qualifies as minor development and would not increase the risk, while the documents say the track would sit on maintained grassland and would not reduce biodiversity. If approved, the railway would run during fair-weather events only, from 10am to 3pm, Tuesday to Saturday. Aerial view of the site from the west looking towards the eastern boundary. (Image: Godmanchester Community Plant Nursery) The design and access statement adds: "The purpose of the proposed Godmanchester Miniature Railway at the Community Plant Nursery is not simply to introduce a visitor attraction. It is to make an existing community-facing site work harder." Huntingdonshire District Council will decide the application later. Aerial view of the north-east corner of the site, and the relationship between the track and the eastern boundary and properties/community orchard beyond. (Image: Godmanchester Community Plant Nursery) At the nursery's Apple Day in October 2025, train rides provided by the Sawtry Miniature Railways Group doubled the team's previous daily record of 200 rides.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Hacker used role at gaming giant to steal over £300k from players
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A hacker who used his role as a content developer at a Cambridgeshire company to steal more than £300,000 worth of "game wealth" has avoided prison. Andrew Lakeman, 32, formerly Jed Sanderson and known in gaming circles as “Mod Jed”, joined British gaming giant Jagex in November 2015. Cambridge-based Jagex is best known for its RuneScape games. In May 2018, Jagex’s player support team noticed suspicious account recovery activity with valuable in-game items, including gold, being taken. The activity stopped briefly so the team initially put it down to a glitch in the system, but it began happening again later that year. They realised the perpetrator was likely to be someone who worked for the company, as accounts were being recovered using information genuine owners would be unlikely to know. Jagex began its own internal investigation, which included creating a curfew for account recovery and modifying the firewall. It made these changes without informing the wider company so as not to alert the virtual thief. The sting worked and the Jagex IT department were able to identify Lakeman’s devices and home address as the source of the illicit activity. Jagex later sacked Lakeman and passed the investigation to Report Fraud, which referred it to Cambridgeshire Police in 2019. Officers found that Lakeman had sold the virtual gold and other valuable in-game items on the black market. Searches of his devices and accounts showed he had received more than £364,829 from cryptocurrency dealers. Messages to his wife showed he planned to make a fortune before leaving Jagex. He also discussed RuneScape accounts worth tens of thousands of pounds. Lakeman was arrested in July 2019 and charged with unauthorised computer access with intent to commit other offences, theft by employee, conceal / disguise / convert / transfer / remove criminal property and acquire criminal property. Lakeman, of Harbour Road, Beadnell, Chathill, Northumberland, later pleaded guilty to the offences and was handed a three-year sentence suspended for two years at Cambridge Crown Court yesterday (3 September). He was also ordered to complete 150 hours of unpaid work and a 25-day rehabilitation activity requirement. Additionally, a proceeds of crime act timetable, due to conclude in February next year, aims to recoup the money Lakeman earned from the thefts. Detective Constable Andrew McKeane, who investigated, said: "This was an incredibly complex and detailed investigation and certainly not one you see every day. "Lakeman was well aware what he was doing was wrong, and the hundreds of thousands of pounds he gained from selling the in-game items is no different to any other theft. "Just because it’s virtual, doesn’t’ mean he shouldn’t face the full force of the law. "I would like to thank my team for their hard work and diligence during what has been an unusual and lengthy investigation." "It is also important to recognise the significant assistance of senior Crown Prosecutor, Samantha Woolley, and Prosecution Counsel, Sarah Gaunt, for their drive and determination, which led to groundbreaking case law that was heard at the Court of Appeal. "Given the rapid growth of online and virtual worlds, the justice system is going to have to keep pace and adapt to these new and emerging crimes." Have you got a story you want to share? Get in touch at oliver.murphy@newsquest.co.uk

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: 86-year-old St Neots care home resident fulfils dream with first helicopter flight
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: An 86-year-old care home resident from St Neots has taken to the skies for the first time. Eileen, who lives at Henbrook House, fulfilled her dream of flying in a helicopter after staff arranged the special trip from Bottisham Airfield Museum near Cambridge. Eileen and her daughter Fiona (Image: Henbrook House) She was joined for the experience by her daughter Fiona, taking in views of the Cambridgeshire countryside, including Ely and Newmarket. James Chandler, customer relationship manager at Henbrook House, said: "We were so happy to have been able to arrange this experience for Eileen and her daughter. Eileen enjoying the flight (Image: Henbrook House) "Trips like this obviously require careful judgement and planning, especially when health and mobility factors make accessibility tricky. "However, wherever it is safe to do so, we try to treat those barriers as problems to be solved rather than reasons not to try." Eileen, who once lived in Australia, often watched helicopters fly overhead and dreamed of seeing the world from above. The helicopter Eileen flew in (Image: Henbrook House) Although she encouraged her daughters to embrace adventure, her own reduced mobility in recent years made it difficult to join them. When staff at Henbrook House asked about an experience she would love to try, the helicopter flight quickly became the top choice. The care home team believes moving into residential care should not limit a person’s ambitions. Their philosophy centres on helping residents achieve long-held dreams and enjoy meaningful, personalised activities. This approach aligns with NICE guidance, which defines meaningful activity in care homes as physical, social or leisure activity tailored to an individual’s needs and preferences. Michael Zinaka, general manager at Henbrook House, said: "Our ambition is to challenge the idea that moving into residential care means stepping back from life. "Instead, a care home should be a secure base from which residents can keep enjoying familiar interests, spend time with their loved ones and try new things. Read more Miniature railway plans submitted for Huntingdonshire community nursery site NHS launches flu jab drive in Cambridgeshire and names who gets a free jab "Eileen’s experience is a wonderful reminder that later life can still be full of anticipation and excitement. "For us, exceptional care is about making those moments possible." Henbrook House, part of the Connaught Care Collection, opened in April 2024. It was named one of the top care homes in the East of England by carehome.co.uk in February 2026, marking its second consecutive year receiving the award.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Plans for up to seven homes near Huntingdonshire village conservation area
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Find, save and share Public Notices that affect you in the  area. The Public Notice Portal carries statutory public notices published in local newspapers and is the fastest and most effective way of finding out what is happening in YOUR neighbourhood. Plans have been submitted for up to seven homes in a Huntingdonshire village. AN Polhill Farm Limited has applied to Huntingdonshire District Council for permission in principle to build the homes on 0.48 hectares of farmland east of Sawtry Road, Glatton. The application seeks permission in principle for between one and seven homes to boost the area’s housing supply. The supporting planning statement says the homes would fit Glatton’s existing built-up area rather than extend the village beyond its established boundary. Plans have been submitted for up to seven homes on a site in Glatton. (Image: Phillips Planning Services Ltd) Read more Huntingdon stalker jailed after 'campaign of harassment' against victim Inquest into death of 'beloved' Cambs mother who died unexpectedly at home Cambridge family issue Jeans for Genes plea after daughter diagnosed at six weeks Free blood pressure checks at Huntingdon surgery as part of national campaign Woman sexually assaulted in Hunts village as police ramp up patrols Phillips Planning Services Ltd drew up the statement, which says the site would "balance existing development on both sides of Sawtry Road". Huntingdonshire District Council currently reports a housing land supply of 3.68 years, below the government’s requirement of five years. The applicant says the shortfall strengthens the case for small housing schemes. The land is currently in agricultural use and is screened from the road by mature trees and vegetation, with residential properties located to the north and west. The site lies adjacent to the Glatton Conservation Area and near White Roses, a Grade II-listed cottage dating from the early 17th century. The statement says the homes would have a "neutral impact" on nearby heritage assets because roadside trees would screen them from the conservation area and listed building. Historic England was consulted but declined to advise on the scheme. In a letter to the council, the organisation said its involvement "would not add value in this case" and recommended seeking input from the council’s own conservation and archaeological specialists. Permission in principle decides whether the site, its use and the scale of development are acceptable. If approved, a further application for technical details consent would be needed before construction could begin. The application is currently under consideration by Huntingdonshire District Council.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Cambridgeshire schoolchildren are back in class, so here are the county council’s key term dates for autumn 2026 and spring and summer 2027. The dates apply to community and voluntary controlled schools, but academies, foundation, trust and voluntary aided schools set their own calendars. Pupils returned this week, and the autumn term runs until Friday, October 23. Read more Inquest into death of 'beloved' Cambs mother who died unexpectedly at home New fitness studio inspired by Florida wellness scene opens in Huntingdonshire Convicted Cambs sex offender jailed after setting up secret accounts Cambridgeshire ‘school streets’ could be enforced with cameras The fascinating history of St Ives island's basket makers Half term runs from Monday, October 26, to Friday, October 30. The second half of the autumn term runs from Monday, November 2, to Friday, December 18. The Christmas holidays run from Monday, December 21, to Friday, January 1. The spring term runs from Monday, January 4, to Friday, February 12, followed by half term from Monday, February 15, to Friday, February 19. The spring term resumes on Monday, February 22, and ends on Thursday, March 25. The Easter holidays run from Friday, March 26, to Friday, April 9. The summer term runs from Monday, April 12, to Friday, May 28, with half term from Monday, May 31, to Friday, June 4. The final part of the summer term runs from Monday, June 7, to Wednesday, July 21. In March 2024, Department for Education guidance said fines must be considered when a child misses five school days through unauthorised absence.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Cambs police receive over 400 domestic abuse calls in one month
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Throughout August, police received more than 400 calls about domestic abuse where they believed someone to be in immediate danger in Cambridgeshire. This equates to an average of 13 urgently graded calls about domestic abuse every single day. A spokesperson for the force said: 'Home is not a safe space for everyone, but we will always be here to help and will continue to work tirelessly to keep victims safe.' They are urging people to report any concerns to them, no matter how small or insignificant they may seem. Advice and support services are available on their domestic abuse web page.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: NHS launches flu jab drive in Cambridgeshire and names who gets a free jab
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: People across Cambridgeshire and Peterborough are being urged to get their flu vaccinations as the NHS begins its annual autumn programme ahead of winter. The NHS has begun its annual autumn flu vaccination programme in Cambridgeshire and Peterborough, offering jabs to children, pregnant women, and other vulnerable groups. From September 1, vaccinations are available for pregnant women, children aged two and three (as of August 31, 2026), and children with certain long-term health conditions through their GP practice. Cali Makewell, strategic vaccination lead at NHS Central East, said: "Flu can be particularly serious for young children and pregnant women, which is why we're encouraging everyone who is eligible to come forward when invited. "Getting vaccinated during pregnancy helps protect both mother and baby, while children's flu vaccination helps protect them from serious illness and reduce the spread of flu to family members and others around them." Parents of school-aged children from Reception to Year 11 will also be asked to give consent for vaccinations delivered in most schools. Pregnant women can receive the vaccine through maternity services, GP practices, or participating community pharmacies. Last winter, more than 2.34 million people were vaccinated against flu across the East of England. The National Booking Service is now open for people aged 65 and over, those aged 18 to 65 with certain health conditions, care home residents, carers, close contacts of people with weakened immune systems, and frontline health and social care workers. Appointments for these groups are available from October 1 and can be booked online, through the NHS App, or by calling 119. Cali said: "If you're aged 65 or over, have a long-term health condition, are a carer, a frontline health or social care worker, or are otherwise eligible, you can book your appointment now. "Getting vaccinated ahead of winter helps protect you, your loved ones and our NHS services during what is often the busiest time of year."

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Fifteen new police officers from diverse backgrounds begin serving Cambridgeshire
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Fifteen new police officers from backgrounds including tennis coaching, teaching and hospitality are set to begin serving communities across Cambridgeshire. The group was welcomed to Cambridgeshire Constabulary by Chief Constable Simon Megicks and will now be deployed to various stations across the county. The recruits, who are on the Police Constable Entry Programme (PCEP), will focus on police skills. The force is currently seeking more applicants for the PCEP, a two-year course with various assessments. More details can be found on their website.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: New rental development in Cambridge offers spacious homes for less
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Sponsored by L&Q L&Q at Virido offers a collection of one-, two- and three-bedroom homes in Trumpington through Intermediate Market Rent, a government-backed scheme helping eligible renters access homes at below local market rates. Set within the growing Great Kneighton neighbourhood, residents can enjoy spacious, modern homes surrounded by green space, while remaining within easy reach of Cambridge city centre and some of the city’s major employment hubs. Whether you’re looking for an extra bedroom, space to work from home or simply more room to live, L&Q at Virido offers homes designed to fit around everyday life. The collection ranges from one-, two- and three-bedroom apartments and duplexes to one-, two- and three-bedroom houses, making it an appealing option for young professionals, couples and families alike. Homes are ready to move into, with an impressive specification on offer. Contemporary kitchens come complete with integrated appliances, alongside sleek bathrooms and en-suites, modern flooring and an allocated parking space with every property – taking some of the hassle out of moving and allowing residents to settle straight into their new home. For renters who have outgrown a traditional city-centre apartment, the larger homes offer the chance to gain that all-important extra space while staying close to Cambridge. Green space is woven into the design of the wider Virido neighbourhood. Homes are arranged in a series of ‘quads’ around shared gardens, creating pockets of landscaped space for residents to enjoy right outside their homes. Every home also has its own private outdoor space, offering even more room to enjoy life outside during the warmer months. Sustainability has been considered throughout the development too, with rainwater harvesting systems designed to reduce water use. Designed to achieve Code for Sustainable Homes Level 5, homes at L&Q at Virido also feature enhanced insulation, mechanical ventilation heat recovery systems and solar PV panels to building roofs, bringing greener features into everyday life. L&Q at Virido offers a collection of one-, two- and three-bedroom homes (Image: L&Q) At L&Q at Virido, gaining more space doesn’t mean giving up the convenience of city living. Cambridge city centre is around a 10-minute drive away, putting its independent shops, cafés, restaurants, historic streets and green spaces within easy reach. For those working locally, the development is less than a mile from Addenbrooke’s Hospital and the Cambridge Biomedical Campus, making it particularly well placed for an easy commute. There are plenty of options for getting around too. The Cambridge Guided Busway and a number of cycle routes are close to the development, while Cambridge Train Station is around 2.1 miles away. Trumpington Park & Ride and the M11 are also a short drive away. At L&Q at Virido, renters have the key opportunity to pay less than they might expect to rent a similar home locally. With homes available through Intermediate Market Rent, a government-backed scheme designed to help make renting more affordable, eligible renters can access homes at up to 80% of local market rent, helping to make monthly housing costs more manageable and potentially leaving more room to save for the future. For those looking for more space without stretching their monthly budget, L&Q at Virido offers the opportunity to rent more for less in desirable Cambridge. To explore the one-, two- and three-bedroom homes currently available at L&Q at Virido and to register your interest, visit lqhomes.com Sponsored by L&Q

news.title: Cambridgeshire bus services to change after combined authority review
news.content: A number of bus services in Cambridgeshire are due to change following a review. Cambridgeshire and Peterborough Combined Authority (CPCA) carried out a review of bus services across the county to ensure the bus network was affordable, sustainable, evidence led and better aligned to passenger need. In Peterborough, the proposed changes include merging services 60 and 61, and introducing different timetables for services 60, 61, 62 and 63. They also include retaining the current loop around Werrington as part of the 62 service, helping residents to continue accessing Werrington centre. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Food recall alert Tesco, Waitrose and Home Bargains shoppers warned to check fridges
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Shoppers are being urged to check their fridges and cupboards after a series of food safety alerts triggered product recalls at major UK supermarkets. The Food Standards Agency (FSA) has issued several “do not eat” warnings covering products sold at retailers including Tesco, Waitrose and Home Bargains, with some potentially posing a health risk. With multiple recalls announced, households are being urged to check their kitchens now to make sure they do not have any of the affected products. Shoppers in Northern Ireland are being urged to check their fridges after two Macroom Buffalo Cheese products were recalled over Listeria concerns. Macroom Buffalo Cheese Products is recalling Mozzarella (125g) and Bocconcini (160g), both with a use-by date of September 7, 2026, after Listeria monocytogenes was found. Customers who have bought the affected cheeses are being told not to eat them, even if they look and smell normal. They should return them to the retailer for a full refund. Friday 28 August - Macroom Buffalo Cheese Products recalls Macroom Buffalo Cheese Mozzarella and Macroom Buffalo Cheese Bocconcini due to contamination with Listeria monocytogenes #FoodAlert https://t.co/zPlJT0mZI4 pic.twitter.com/rUKzpFmBVi — Food Standards Agency (@foodgov) August 28, 2026 Listeria symptoms can include a high temperature, muscle aches, chills, sickness and diarrhoea. In rare cases, infection can cause serious complications including meningitis. Those most vulnerable include over-65s, pregnant women and unborn babies, young babies and people with weakened immune systems. Shoppers are being urged to check their fridges after a small number of filled wraps were recalled over possible E. coli contamination. The company said: "As part of our routine testing, we have identified a potential food safety issue affecting a small number of our wrap products. "We are working closely with the authorities and our customers to recall the affected products. "Consumer safety remains our highest priority. We are sorry for any concern or inconvenience this may cause." The recall affects Snacksters Chicken Fajita Wrap, Snacksters Hoi Sin Wrap, East Street Deli Sweet Chilli Chicken Wrap and Target a Snack Chicken Fajita Wrap. All use-by dates up to and including September 5, 2026 are affected. The Food Standards Agency (FSA) said the products could contain Shiga toxin-producing E. coli (STEC), which can cause severe diarrhoea, including bloody diarrhoea, and abdominal pain. In some cases, infection can lead to haemolytic uraemic syndrome (HUS), a serious condition that can cause kidney failure and can be fatal. Friday 21 August - Summit Foods is recalling various products because of possible contamination with Shiga-toxin producing E. coli (STEC) #FoodAlert https://t.co/MGnLjK0Al6 pic.twitter.com/OMs3rdsvoY — Food Standards Agency (@foodgov) August 21, 2026 If you have bought any of the affected wraps, do not eat them. Instead, dispose of the product and email sales@summitfoods.co.uk with proof of purchase, stating when and where it was bought, to request a refund. The recall is listed by the FSA under reference FSA-PRIN-40-2026. A.Vogel Ltd is recalling Rapunzel bioSnacky Das Original Red Clover Seeds for Sprouts and Seedlings because of the presence of Shiga toxin-producing E.coli. Symptoms can include severe diarrhoea, abdominal pain and occasionally haemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS), a serious condition that can lead to kidney failure and can be fatal. The affected products come in 30g packs, have a batch code of 11293 and a best before date of December 2028. Monday 8 August - A.Vogel Ltd recalls Rapunzel bioSnacky Das Original Red Clover – Seeds for Sprouts and Seedlings due to contamination with E. coli (STEC) #foodalert https://t.co/vR2Mt6161P pic.twitter.com/zritLd5U5v — Food Standards Agency (@foodgov) August 10, 2026 A spokesman for the Food Standards Agency warned: “A.Vogel Ltd is recalling the above product. Point of sale notices will be displayed in all retail stores that are selling this product and/or on their website. These notices explain to customers why the product is being recalled and tell them what to do if they have bought the product. “If you have bought the above product, do not grow it or consume the sprouts or seedlings. Instead, return it to where you bought it from for a full refund. “Symptoms can include severe diarrhoea (including bloody diarrhoea), abdominal pain and occasionally haemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS), a serious condition that can lead to kidney failure and can be fatal. “If you are experiencing these symptoms, you should stay away from work, school or nursery until you have stopped having symptoms for at least 48 hours to avoid passing it on to others.” A Rapunzel spokesman added: "We are very sorry for this incident and sincerely apologise. "Please be assured that we are doing everything we possibly can to resolve this matter. "We hope you will continue to place your trust in us." Crisps sold at Home Bargains have been recalled, with the Food Standards Agency (FSA) warning shoppers of a potential health risk. ASR Solutions Ltd has recalled the Lays Sour Cream & Dill Crisps sold in Home Bargains stores in the UK, because of a labelling error. The crisps contain milk and wheat (gluten) which are not mentioned on the label, meaning they are a “possible health risk” to anyone with an allergy or intolerance to the ingredients. The affected products come in 125g packets and have best before dates up to and including October 31. Friday 31 July 2026 - ASR Solutions Ltd recalls Lay's Sour Cream & Dill Crisps #FoodAllergy https://t.co/sx7VuhfXwi pic.twitter.com/Su9jxthEaG — Food Standards Agency (@foodgov) July 31, 2026 An FSA spokesman warned: “ASR Solutions Ltd is recalling the above product from customers and has been advised to contact the relevant allergy support organisations, which will tell their members about the recall. “The company has also issued a recall notice to its customers. These notices explain to customers why the product is being recalled and tell them what to do if they have bought the product. “If you have bought this product, do not eat it. Instead, return it to the store from which you bought the product for a full refund or contact  support@home.bargains  if you require further information.” A Home Bargains statement added: “If you have bought Lays Sour Cream & Dill Crisps as detailed above and you have an allergy, intolerance or sensitivity to milk or wheat, do not consume it. “Check if you have bought the affected best before dates. Only these codes are affected. “Return any affected product to your local Home Bargains store for a full refund or contact support@home.bargains if you require information. “We apologise for any inconvenience caused.” A range of chocolate products sold in England, Scotland and Wales have been removed from UK shelves due to health concerns. Bon Bons Wholesale Ltd has recalled various chocolate products due to the concerns, telling shops stocking the items to “remove them from sale”, while the Food Standards Agency (FSA) has told shoppers, “Do not eat”. The items have been recalled because they may contain milk and soy which are not mentioned on the label, making them a potential health risk for anyone with allergies. An FSA spokesman said: “These products contain milk and soya making them a possible health risk for anyone with an allergy or intolerance to milk or milk constituents and/or an allergy to soya.” 25th July - Bon Bons Wholesale Ltd recalls various chocolate products because of undeclared milk and soya #FoodAllergy https://t.co/WrIP1T09q5 pic.twitter.com/ps2AV2kcLh — Food Standards Agency (@foodgov) July 25, 2026 These are the Bon Bons Wholesale Ltd items affected by the recall: An FSA spokesman said: “Bon Bons Wholesale Ltd is recalling the above products from customers and has been advised to contact the relevant allergy support organisations, which will tell their members about the recall. “The company has also issued a point-of-sale notice to its customers. These notices explain to customers why the products are being recalled and tell them what to do if they have bought the products. “If you have bought the above products and have an allergy to milk and/or soya do not eat them. Instead, return them to the store you purchased them from for a full refund. “For more information, or to receive a full refund, please contact enquiries@bonbons.co.uk or call 01937 840681.” A Bon Bons Wholesale Ltd statement added: “We take our responsibility to consumers extremely seriously and always aim to ensure the highest possible standards of product safety. “We are sorry for any inconvenience or disappointment this product recall may cause you.” Shoppers at Tesco and Waitrose have been issued a “do not eat” warning after a Gü dessert was recalled. The Gü Double Sea Salted Caramel Frozen Dessert, sold at Tesco and Waitrose, has been removed from supermarket shelves because it may contain hazelnuts and soya not mentioned on the label. As a result, the dessert is a health risk to anyone with an allergy to nuts or soya. The affected product has a lot number of 126135 and a best before date of June 30, 2027. A spokesman for the Food Standards Agency (FSA) said: “Gü is recalling the above product from customers and has been advised to contact the relevant allergy support organisations, which will tell their members about the recall. “These notices explain to customers why the product is being recalled and tell them what to do if they have bought the product. “If you have bought the above product and have an allergy to hazelnuts (nuts) and/or soya do not eat it. Instead return it to the store from where it was bought for a full refund. “No receipt required. For more information, please contact recall@gupuds.com .” A Gü spokesman added: “The issue is limited to a very small number of products (believed to be less than 10 units). However, as a precautionary measure and in line with our commitment to consumer safety, the affected date code is being recalled. “We have taken proactive steps to further mitigate the issue, including strengthened allergen and packing controls within production. “We believe the majority of consumers who purchased the affected products will already have been contacted or notified.” Recommended reading If there is a problem with a food product that means it should not be sold, then it might be 'withdrawn' (taken off the shelves) or 'recalled' (when customers are asked to return the product). The FSA issues Product Withdrawal Information Notices and Product Recall Information Notices to let consumers and local authorities know about problems associated with food. In some cases, a 'Food Alert for Action' is issued. This provides local authorities with details of specific actions to be taken on behalf of consumers.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Drivers warned simple parking mistake could leave them with £1,200 repair bill
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: The last few months has seen some extreme weather in the UK from heatwaves to droughts and now drivers are being warned about the weather’s effect on trees. That’s because it’s easy to park under a tree and expect no damage to be done to your car, but you could get into some bother if a branch comes loose and lands on it. With the sun still making an appearance, you might choose to park under a tree to keep your car cool, but you’ll need to be aware of the risk of branches breaking without warning, says Graham Conway, managing director at Select Car Leasing. He says a falling tree branch can cause serious damage to a car and risk injuring a driver or passengers. Conway added: “In the hot weather, it’s understandable that motorists will look for any shady spot to park their car to try and keep it cooler. “But with prolonged dry, hot weather, tree branches may be weakened and break without warning.” He explains: “Falling branches, particularly from large trees, can cause significant structural damage to a car, which could cost motorists thousands. “Heavy branches could dent the body, shatter the windscreen or break side mirrors. “Even damage from smaller branches can result in dents and scratches to the body of the car. “Look out for trees that have grey, brittle wood or bark that is peeling off, as this is often a sign that the tree is dying, causing the branches to dry out and snap off. “Trees that have cracks or splits, especially at the point where a branch joins the trunk, may also indicate that a tree is dying. “However, there aren’t always warning signs, so it’s best to be extra cautious.” He said trees can also experience ‘summer branch drop syndrome’, which can happen without visible signs. Conway added: “This most often occurs when sudden summer rain follows a long, dry period. “Insurance will typically cover any damage as a result of an ‘act of God’ however, if the tree was on council or private land and was already in a dangerous state, you may be able to recover your excess costs from whoever owns it. “If the tree was clearly deteriorating before it fell, or the owner had been warned and failed to act, they could be considered negligent. “If you think the owner was at fault, photograph the tree's condition, keep any evidence, and raise it with your insurer.” “As a guide, UK bonnet repairs can range from around £50 to £150 for minor dents, £300 to £700 for a replacement bonnet and £500 to £1,200+ for major structural damage, while comprehensive car insurance can cover falling trees and branches during storms, depending on the policy.” Smith added: “Drivers should also be careful about parking under trees during windy or wet weather, as weakened branches may not be obvious from ground level. “If a storm is forecast, it is always better to move the car somewhere more open, even if that means walking a little further.” Recommended reading: The expert adds that there are a few more things you should bear in mind when parking under a tree: Smith explains: “Sap and droppings in particular can mark the paintwork, and if they are baked on by the sun, they can become much harder to remove without causing scratches.” He also shared some more spots you should think twice about parking close to: He said you can expect an increased risk of debris, dust or accidental damage or a bigger chance of dents, scratches or broken windows in these areas. Concluding, he advises drivers to be aware of where they are parking: “The safest approach is to look up and around before leaving your car. “If there is anything above, beside or nearby that could fall, blow over, leak, mark the paintwork or limit visibility, it is probably worth finding another space.” Do you have any other parking tips for drivers? Let us know in the comments.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Citizens Advice Rural Cambs gives tips on how to deal with your debts
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Meghan Hawthorne, debt caseworker at Citizens Advice Rural Cambs, talks about how debt and money problems in general can feel extremely overwhelming It is important to remember that you do not have to face this alone and we are there to support you. The biggest step forward is reaching out and asking for help. We know how nerve-wracking this can be, so in the case that you want to try and work things out yourself, or gather the relevant information before asking for debt advice, I wanted to give you some self-help tips on how to do this: Building your Budget: Knowing how much you have coming in and how much you have going out will show you how much money you have left over at the end of the month. · Start to gather bank statements, wage slips, benefit letters/information, etc. · You can build a budget sheet on paper, online or through a budgeting app. One we recommend is the online Money Helper Budget Planner: https://www.moneyhelper.org.uk/en/everyday-money/budgeting/budget-planner Collecting Information on Your Debts: Knowing exactly what you owe to whom will show you your debt total and show you who you need to be contacting about your debts. · Gather statements, bills, contracts, letters, etc. Getting your credit reports (TransUnion, Experian and Equifax) will show you what money you have borrowed, paid back and owe. · Details to collect: o Who the creditor is (who you owe money to); o How much you owe; o What stage the debt is at (when did you miss the first payment and what has the creditor done to get the money back); o Your account/reference number. Contacting Creditors: It can be a good idea to contact your creditors, explain that you are trying to deal with the debt and ask them to: · Confirm the details of the debts. · Put a pause on chasing you until you have all your information gathered and work out what you need to do. · Stop adding interest and charges, which increase the debt. IMPORTANT: If you believe your debt(s) have surpassed the limitation period (6 years), please contact us before contacting your creditors. Priority and Non-Priority Debts: Priority debts have more serious consequences and can cause particularly serious problems if you do not do anything about them. · Priority Debts can include: rent and mortgage (or secured loan) arrears, council tax arrears, energy arrears, TV licence, court fines, etc. · Non-Priority Debts can include: credit cards, catalogues, unsecured (including payday) loans, unpaid water bills, money borrowed from family and friends, etc. When to Ask for Help: · If you are struggling to deal with your priority debts and/or you have more than one priority debt and don’t know which one to deal with first; · If you have completed your budget and don’t have money left over at the end of the month; · If you want to have a look at ways of potentially increasing your income and reducing your expenditure; · You have received court paperwork and/or have been contacted/visited by bailiffs. If you decide that you need to contact us for further support, our advisers will always be happy to help and guide you in taking the relevant next steps. You can contact us on Freephone 0808 278 7807: 9.30am-3.30pm Monday, Thursday, and Friday, and from 9.30am-7pm Tuesday and Wednesday, or head to our website https://www.citizensadviceruralcambs.org.uk/ for more information.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Urgent repairs needed at historic church threatened by water damage
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A council has agreed to help fund “urgent repairs” to a village church amid safety concerns. St Andrew’s Church in Wimpole had already spent £14,000 of their own money repairing the aging building from damage caused by water ingress and deteriorating masonry. The Grade II listed building is owned by the Diocese of Ely and, as well as providing church services, also hosts concerts, community events and art exhibitions. But the church’s future has been put at risk with water damage causing staining, plaster deterioration and even falling debris. The church applied for £2,000 of funding from South Cambridgeshire District Council’s community chest to continue repairs. This will also go towards restoring two historic monuments – reattaching the lion to the effigy of Thomas Chicheley and cleaning and refixing the brass plaque to Reginald York. The Church Is Located On The Wimpole Estate. Credit: Google Maps This will cost £3,719 while the roof and masonry work will cost £11,234. The church said they will meet their remaining costs through fundraising activities, existing reserves, private donations and applications to external funders. They have submitted applications to the Cambridge Historic Churches Trust and the Heritage Lottery Fund – and secured a £1,000 private donation, with indications of future private support. Council officers recommended approving the funding as it would support “the continued use of a well-used community facility and heritage site, ensuring it remains accessible to residents, visitors and researchers for years to come”. They said the repairs were necessary to stop the building deteriorating further and to improve public safety. The council approved the funding.

Being only one, he still has a lot to learn about the world around him - but with the right owner, staff think he would thrive. A spokesperson for the centre said: “Lloyd really is a gentle giant and we all adore him. It’s heartbreaking that he hasn’t had the easiest start in his short life. Since arriving with us, he has made fantastic progress and is becoming increasingly relaxed with new people, especially when introductions are calm and at his own pace. Once he gets to know you, Lloyd's affectionate and loyal nature really shines through. “Our gorgeous boy is looking for an adult-only home where he can enjoy a predictable routine and continue building his confidence. A quieter home in a rural or semi-rural setting, with peaceful walking routes and fewer day-to-day distractions, would suit him perfectly and help him continue making positive strides. “He would be best as the only pet in the home. While he enjoys seeing other dogs from a comfortable distance, he can sometimes find close encounters a little overwhelming. Being the centre of someone's world will allow him to keep developing his confidence and create a strong bond with his new family. “Lloyd has so much potential and is ready for the next chapter of his life. With patient, understanding adopters, plenty of encouragement, and a calm environment, we're confident he'll continue to blossom into the devoted, loving companion we already know he is.” Experience with large or Mastiff-type breeds would be an advantage, as Lloyd is a big, strong lad. Despite his size, he has made lovely progress with his lead walking and enjoys getting out and exploring. He's becoming more settled on walks and is continuing to learn that the world isn't such a scary place. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: High street chain hosts closing down sale with £1 items in major restructuring plan
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A popular stationery shop chain has launched a closing-down sale with customers able to get some final bargains as prices start from just £1. TG Jones, formerly known as WH Smith, has secured court approval for a major restructuring, which is expected to lead to the closure of around 150 stores and affect hundreds of jobs. In July, TG Jones’ restructuring plan was approved by the High Court in a move which will save the business from insolvency. Closing-down sale signs have appeared in TG Jones shops across the UK, with customers also able to shop its sale online. TG Jones’ website is giving customers the chance to buy items for as little as £1, with everything from gift bags to books and toys included in the closing-down sale. The retailer warned online customers: “Don't miss your last chance to buy and grab your favourites for less today - once items in our Sale are gone, they really are gone forever!” Online offers include: It has been announced that stores in Essex (Basildon, Southend and Maldon) will close in September and October, and the Stroud store is also hosting a sale for customers before it leaves the high street. The chain of shops was renamed to TG Jones last year after being bought by Modella, while WH Smith kept its group of stores in travel locations such as airports and train stations. A post shared by TGJones (@tgjonesuk) There are around 450 TG Jones stores with 4,700 staff, mostly in the UK. It previously warned that the overhaul would put jobs at risk, but didn’t disclose how many workers will be affected. In July, Alex Willson, chief executive of TG Jones, said: “We welcome the court’s approval of our restructuring plan. “This decision allows us to move ahead with our turnaround strategy. “The plan protects the substantial core of the store estate and makes TG Jones a stronger, more sustainable business. “We are incredibly grateful to all the colleagues, partners and stakeholders who engaged constructively throughout the process, and to Modella Capital for its continued financial commitment.” Recommended reading: Tom Smith KC, for TG Jones, said that the “working assumption” is that around 150 stores will close as a result of the plans, as landlords who do not wish to accept the reduced rate can choose to terminate the lease. He also said the company has suffered from “long-term sales decline”, exacerbated by high inflation, increased online shopping, reduced consumer spending, with higher labour costs and taxes. The rebranding from WH Smith has also damaged sales, he added. Is your local TG Jones store closing its doors? Let us know in the comments.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Unpaid carers invited to help shape future support services
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Unpaid carers in Cambridgeshire are being invited to help shape the future of support services. Cambridgeshire County Council is gathering insights from carers and those with lived experience of caring to help design future adult carer support services in the county. A series of workshops will be held between September 2026 and March 2027, offering carers a chance to influence service priorities, delivery models, and commissioning plans. Graham Wilson, chair of the council’s Adults and Health Committee, said: "Unpaid carers play a vital role in supporting loved ones and helping people live independently. "Their contribution is often unseen, but makes a huge difference to individuals, families and communities across Cambridgeshire. "We are committed to enabling full and healthy lives for all residents by helping to build strong community ties and supporting independent living. "That means listening to the people who use and rely on our services. "Carers understand better than anyone the challenges and opportunities that come with caring responsibilities, and their experiences are invaluable in helping us shape future support. "This is an opportunity for carers to have a real say in how services are developed. "I would encourage anyone with experience of caring to get involved and help us ensure support meets the needs of carers now and in the future." The first workshop will take place on Friday, September 18, from 10.30am to 12.30pm at Huntingdon Library. Attendees will discuss what future carer services should prioritise and the outcomes they want to see. This work also supports The Big Conversation on Care, which launched on 29 July and is the largest public conversation about adult social care in a generation. To take part or request more information, email Commissioning.FPTeam@cambridgeshire.gov.uk.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: World record attempt to test 100 men for prostate cancer in one day
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Eaton Socon Health Centre in St Neots will host an attempt to set a new world record on Saturday September 5. At least 100 men are expected to receive free prostate cancer tests and examinations in a single day. Miss Jyoti Shah MBE, a surgeon at North West Anglia NHS Foundation Trust, said: "Prostate cancer is a silent killer, but it is a cancer that we can cure if we pick it up early enough. "It is the most common cancer in men in the UK, with one in eight being diagnosed as some point in their lives – and for men from an Afro-Caribbean heritage, the risk is one in four. "I am so very proud of and thankful to my team for their dedication and giving their time to support this important community event – and to our Hospitals' Charity for meeting the cost of the PSA tests." The event is supported by the St Neots Prostate Cancer Support Group and Purple Horizons, a community interest company based in St Neots. The current registered GuinnessWorld Records for men signing up for testing in eight hours is 258 in Egypt in 2024. Each PSA blood test costs around £3.50, with funding provided by the North West Anglia Hospitals’ Charity. Miss Shah and her team will register each patient on the hospital system, review medical histories, and carry out blood tests and physical examinations. All services are offered free of charge and on a voluntary basis. Patients will receive their results directly, and their GPs will also be notified. Further follow-up information will be provided as needed. The event aims to raise awareness of prostate cancer and encourage more men to get tested.

The event will be a unique opportunity for participants aged 16 and over to learn self-defence principles based on more than 50 years of martial arts experience. The seminar is not just about learning new skills; it's also about raising funds for the Sweetlove Cancer Nurse, a cause that will benefit from every penny raised during the event. Martial arts seminar raises funds for cancer nursing support (Image: Inspired Martial Arts) Stephen Sweetlove is a martial arts expert with several high-level grades, including 6th Dan Judo, 6th Dan Ju-Jitsu, and 5th Dan Taiho Jutsu. Participants will learn about Defendu, a practical self-defence system developed in the 1920s known for its application in real-world encounters. This inclusive approach reflects the philosophy of Inspired Martial Arts, which emphasises the importance of confidence, discipline, and awareness in effective self-defence. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Amazing former Addenbrooke's Hospital patient Grace wins The Piano TV show
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A former Addenbrooke’s Hospital patient who lost her fingers and lower legs after contracting meningitis as a child has won Channel 4’s The Piano. Grace Matthews, 19, received a standing ovation after performing in the show’s final at Birmingham’s Symphony Hall. Pop singer Mika named her the winner after telling the audience that one performer had been able to “take the collective consciousness of thousands of strangers” and suspend it “in mid-air” through music. Grace, from Norfolk, said after hearing her name announced: “I’m shaking. I don’t know what to say. That’s insane. I did not think that would be the outcome at all, but thank you all, all, so much for coming and watching and thank you to the best contestants and partners I could ask for!” Grace Matthews, aged three (Image: CUH) Grace was three when she developed a temperature in January 2011 and was taken to Norfolk and Norwich University Hospital before being transferred to Addenbrooke’s in Cambridge. Tests confirmed meningitis and meningococcal septicaemia. She spent nine days in intensive care and became critically ill, with surgery ultimately necessary to save her life. She lost all her fingers and both lower legs. Now using prosthetic legs, Grace plays the piano using her palm, half a thumb and the stub of a little finger. Her repertoire includes music by Pink, Adele, Queen and Bruce Springsteen, and she arranges the music herself. Her mother, Vicky Matthews, said the family were “completely overwhelmed and incredibly proud”. She added: “To see how far she has come is something we will never take for granted. “We will always be grateful to the incredible team at Norfolk and Norwich University Hospitals Foundation Trust and Addenbrooke’s who saved her life.” During Grace’s recovery, her former Addenbrooke’s music therapist Dawn Loombe and hospital play specialists became a central part of her day. Grace Matthews and her former Addenbrooke’s music therapist Dawn Loombe. (Image: CUH) Despite bandages on her hands, Grace enjoyed playing eight-octave rainbow bells while Ms Loombe played the accordion or guitar. After returning home to her parents, Vicky and Brian, and brother Tom, she progressed from a small electric keyboard to a full-sized electric piano. Ms Loombe supported Grace’s application for The Piano, and the teenager first appeared in the programme in June, performing Ludovico Einaudi’s contemporary classical piece Experience. Ms Loombe, now working part-time for Suffolk Music Therapy Services after retiring from Addenbrooke’s, said: “From the first time I met Grace, it was obvious that she was incredibly resilient and musically gifted. “She loved all the instruments, particularly the accordion, guitar, piano keyboard and the rainbow bells. She wanted to play everything and could copy melodies in no time.” Grace was selected for the final after performing in front of travellers at Birmingham New Street Station during filming for the series. Her winning performance at Symphony Hall moved the 2,000-strong audience, with viewers watching her receive the show’s top prize. You can listen to her music on Spotify.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Ex-teacher slams school's uniform rule as pupils face isolation over haircuts
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary:
A Huntingdonshire school has apologised after children who opted for certain hairstyles risked being placed in isolation. Longsands Academy, in St Neots, told parents that students would be placed in "reset" if their haircut or hair colour was not deemed to be an acceptable style. According to the school's recently updated uniform policy, "harsh or dramatic contrast between the top of the hair and the sides" is banned. Patterns shaved into a scholar's hair or eyebrows, including an artificial parting, and "high or flamboyant hairstyles" are also outlawed. Meanwhile, skin fades where the pupil's hair is below a grade one and hair that is "teased, backcombed or covered in excessive product" are prohibited. For girls, hair "must be in a conventional and understated style" with hair clips or hair bands either "black or navy blue" in colour. Styles involving large bunches, buns or ponytails on top of the head "obscuring the views of pupils sitting behind" are banned. Under the rule, pupils would remain in isolation until parents grant permission for them to visit a hairdresser to have the hairstyle "rectified". The strict measure sparked a backlash among parents, with people describing the diktat as "concerning". Read more Cambs paedophile, 67, told young girl 'not to tell anyone' about sexual activity
    New 3G football pitch approved despite fears it would make noise problem worse
    Seven NHS children angle a catch at fishing lake
    Boy, three, injured in crocodile enclosure at Cambs zoo discharged from hospital
    Hunts zoo hosts exclusive after-hours event for children and families A former teacher at Longsands, who asked to remain anonymous, claimed the policy is "highly focussed on the ethnic minority population". They told The Hunts Post: "It is worrying that they are allowed to even suggest such requirements of students to all look a clone of one another and not celebrate difference. "The school has taken a significant directional shift since I was there. Focusing more on the policing of children than the teaching and ensuring learning is exciting. "With the booklet learning and scripted narrative, the policy around policing hair styles doesn’t surprise me - what does is the heavily racial focus of such a policy. "I think this policy, being so heavily drawn to focus on minorities could see for a significant rise in racial issues." Longsands Academy in St Neots is run by the Astrea Academy Trust (Image: Street View) The ex-teacher added the policy "removes individualisation and celebrates difference, diversity and culture." It also focuses "a lens on minority groups as being ‘other’ and needing to conform to fit in. This is not the message a school should be sending youth of today," they said. Meanwhile, one parent has taken aim at an illustration of six pupils with hair styles deemed "inappropriate" which accompanies the school's uniform policy. Of the six images featured, four appear to depict students from an ethnic minority background. "I find this concerning because it raises questions about how the policy was developed and whether the examples being used are fair and representative," they said. "Hair can have important cultural and ethnic significance, and policies concerning hairstyles need to be applied consistently and sensitively to all pupils." The parent added they have also sought clarification on how the police applied to pupils who are non-binary. A spokesperson for Astrea Academy Trust, which runs Longsands Academy, said: "We have recently updated our uniform policy to reduce the number of branded items students are required to have this academic year. "As part of this, we updated our haircut policy with illustrations to make clear the sorts of patterns that are not acceptable. “We have listened carefully to the views of parents who told us that these illustrations suggested that certain hairstyles such as cornrows were banned, which was not our intention. "We have worked closely with parents and carers and apologise that the policy was not clear." They added: "We will be sending out an update for families and students shortly. The Driver and Vehicle Licensing Agency (DVLA) is reminding drivers to check their own plates meet the required specifications. Plates that do not comply can lead to a fine and an MOT failure. The DVLA said: “Number plates (also known as licence plates) must show your registration number correctly. You cannot rearrange letters or numbers, or alter them so that they’re hard to read. "You could be fined up to £1,000 and your vehicle will fail its MOT test if you drive with incorrectly displayed number plates." These are the rules you should be aware of around licence plates from the DVLA. The number plates on your vehicle must: The characters must not be removable or reflective. If your number plates were fitted after 1 September 2021, they must also be a single shade of black. Your number plates can also: Graham Conway, Managing Director at Select Car Leasing , said: “Characters must not be removable or reflective, however, your number plates can have 3D (raised) characters, display certain flags, symbols and identifiers and display a green flash, if you have a zero-emission vehicle. “It’s important to drivers to understand the nuances of what’s required for their licence plates as even the smallest modifications could make it illegal. For example, 3D characters are allowed on licence plates, but if the raised letters are not black or have a reflective coating on them, this could make them illegal. Recommended Reading: “It’s also important for drivers to understand that any modifications around their licence plate, that could make it unreadable, are also considered illegal. “For example, licence plate lights must be white – not tinted blue or any other colour – and need to illuminate the plate evenly without causing any shadows. Mistakenly believing it was the victim, an argument ensued outside. He produced a knife and stabbed the man in the abdomen, before leaving the scene and discarding the weapon behind some locked gates in Geneva Street. The victim underwent surgery, was placed in an induced coma and required further treatment for several weeks before being discharged. Stimson, of Greenham, Bretton, Peterborough, admitted assault causing grievous bodily harm without intent and possession of a knife in public. On Friday (August 28) at Cambridge Crown Court he was jailed for 16 months. DC John Pentney said: “Stimson’s shocking actions were completely disproportionate for something as trivial as the bell being used on his scooter. "Stabbing someone like this is extremely reckless and we could easily have been dealing with a murder investigation. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Job with The Co-operative Bank returned my confidence after Centerpoint support
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A young person who experienced homelessness says a job with The Co-operative Bank returned his ‘confidence’. Michael, spent most of his life in care. However, after he returned home from university his relationship broke down with his foster parents – forcing him into sofa surfing and eventually on to the streets. After a few months, he got in contact with Centrepoint, who were able to place him into accommodation and help him find a job. It was here that Michael started working at The Co-operative Bank, through it’s Brick by Brick scheme, and he hasn’t looked back since. He said: “Over two years I applied for 400 jobs. It was demoralising because I really wanted to work but couldn’t as employers would either say I was too experienced or not experienced enough. “Thankfully, Centrepoint and The Co-operative Bank were able to support me into this job now and I love it. Everyone’s friendly and supportive and it’s given me a purpose, as opposed to just existing.” Brick by Brick, launched earlier this year, is a pioneering early careers programme, designed to support young people into sustainable work and move on from homelessness for good. It provides a steady, structured journey starting with employability workshops, and then progressing to the Get Set Go Programme which provides six days classroom learning, mock interviews, professional behaviour guidance, and an introduction to the Bank’s values. After this, a young person will then complete work experience at the Bank which, if successful, is followed by an employment offer, removing the pressure of formal interviews. The program ends with an optional apprenticeship and keep in touch days, designed to improve preparedness between a job offer and start date. The initiative has had 35 young people participating in various steps so far with several securing permanent employment in the Bank’s Contact Centre. Michael is one of these, and discussing the skills it has given him, he said: “Communication, multitasking, timekeeping, but most importantly, confidence. “I’ve gone from thinking ‘Why would a company want me’ to now thinking ‘Why wouldn’t they’.” With over one million young people currently not in education or employment, Brick by Brick is reshaping conversations about homelessness by refusing to define young people by their experiences, instead investing in their potential and honouring their needs. “By meeting young people where they’re at, we can close the opportunity gap that holds too many back from reaching their potential,” said Anna Cuskin, the Bank’s Social Impact Lead. “Everyone deserves the chance to succeed. With the right support, young people can gain confidence, find meaningful employment and build a future beyond homelessness.” A man who was at risk of homelessness has told us how a new home gave him a ‘sense of purpose.’ Kai, 22, was living with his dad before overcrowding at home forced him to find somewhere else to live, he said: “It was a really worrying time. I didn’t know where to go or who to turn to.” Fortunately, Kai was able to get in contact with Centrepoint where through the Rent Deposits Scheme, funded by Nationwide Building Society, he was able to find a place in a House In Multiple Occupation (HMO). “It’s given me the stability to rebuild my life and slowly I'm getting back on track. “One day I'd like to live in a house of my own, by a river, on my own plot of land, and do what I want with it. “That’s my dream and I feel like if I keep sticking at it, I’ll be able to eventually achieve it.” However, young people in Kai’s situation may not be so fortunate – research by Centrepoint has found there has been a 10% fall in HMOs since 2019, with 458,000 in 24/25 compared to 510, 776 in 19/20. When asked if he had any advice for young people going through something similar, Kai said: “Don't give up. It might be hard, but right now, your best bet is to keep pushing forward and look for any form of help where you possibly can. Just keep going.” (Image: Centrepoint) The Prime Minister’s pledge to end rough sleeping has been given an early boost after the number of young people sleeping rough in London dropped by almost half. Between April and June 2026, 202 18–25-year-olds in London were recorded as sleeping rough. This was a 45% decrease from the same quarter last year when 368 young people were reported. The youth homelessness charity Centrepoint said this was cause for celebration and called the number proof that the Prime Minister’s pledge could be achieved. Lisa Doyle, the charity’s Head of Policy and Public Affairs, said: “London is providing the blueprint for what can be achieved when political leaders has the vision and intent to end street homelessness. “These figures are a real cause for celebration, but the job is not done. The Mayor of London and the Government must continue these efforts until rough sleeping is reduced to as close to zero as possible, and anyone forced onto the streets is helped off them quickly. However, the charity warned that ending street sleeping alone is not enough. “We must also remember that homelessness does not begin and end with rough sleeping.” Lisa said, “For every person on the streets, many thousands more are living in insecure or unsafe situations. To avoid reversing this positive trend, the Government must now also address the causes and consequences of those experiences too, and step up efforts to prevent homelessness.” A charity has warned that homeless people’s lives are ‘at risk’ due to the past few months of high temperatures. It comes after August saw another flurry of heatwaves – regularly rising over 30 degrees across the country. The UK’s leading youth homelessness charity, Centrepoint, believes council should do more to protect those sleeping rough when it’s this hot. Lisa Doyle, Head of Policy and Public Affairs, said: “This weather is life threatening for those forced to sleep on the streets. “And while many councils do activate protocols to protect those sleeping rough, there is no legal requirement for local authorities to provide shelter for everyone during severe weather. This must change.” “Ultimately, street homelessness is just the tip of the iceberg – the best way to keep people safe is to reduce homelessness however it is experienced.”
