summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: The fascinating history of St Ives island's basket makers
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Keith Grimwade, Chair of the Friends group, describes the willow-weaving heritage of Holt Island Nature Reserve Osiers, the type of willow used for weaving, were grown on Holt Island from the 1720s to the 1920s. They give the island its name – ‘Holt’ is a local word for a plantation, especially an osier plantation. There was a big demand for willow wands (also known as ‘withies’ or ‘rods’) to make different types of baskets, and products such as filters for fire engine hoses and sieves for straining fruit in jam factories. In 1877 John Harrison founded ‘Harrison and Son, Willow Growers and Basket Makers of St Ives’. The firm prospered and became one of the largest growers of willow in the country. It had several osier plantations along the river, including Holt Island, and totalling 45 acres. Harrisons developed their own hybrid willow, ideal for basket work, a cross between Salix viminalis and Salix triandra. The willow wands were cut by men over the winter. In the spring the firm employed 70-80 women to remove the bark from the wands – ‘stripping the willow’, a call you may have heard when country dancing! From March to June men were employed to hoe between the lines of osiers. The willow wands on Holt Island were sorted, bundled and then taken by barge to The Quay, downstream of the town bridge. It was then transported by horse and cart to the Harrison’s workshop in Filbert’s Walk (now demolished). John’s son Charles, and then his grandson Jack, followed him into the business. One of their biggest contracts was making the sorting baskets for the Post Office. This was ‘square work’, which is much more difficult than making a round basket. The business closed in 1970, unable to compete with the introduction of plastic. But by then they had made over 30,000 potato baskets! Jack described basket making ‘as a work of art’. Fortunately, there are still people who have learnt, and pass on, this ancient skill. Join us on Holt Island on Heritage Open Day on Saturday, 12th September, when John Conkey of the British Basket Makers Association will be demonstrating traditional basket-making techniques from 10.30 am to 3 pm. There may be a chance for you to have a go at weaving, too. We will also have a display of Harrison baskets, kindly lent to us by Jack’s daughter, Charlotte.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Cambridgeshire bus services to change after combined authority review
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: A number of bus services in Cambridgeshire are due to change following a review. Cambridgeshire and Peterborough Combined Authority (CPCA) carried out a review of bus services across the county to ensure the bus network was affordable, sustainable, evidence led and better aligned to passenger need. In Peterborough, the proposed changes include merging services 60 and 61, and introducing different timetables for services 60, 61, 62 and 63. They also include retaining the current loop around Werrington as part of the 62 service, helping residents to continue accessing Werrington centre. Service 60 runs between Peterborough Queensgate Bus Station and Orton Northgate, while 61 runs between Queensgate and Newark Sainsbury’s, 62 runs between Queensgate and Maxey, and 63 runs between Queensgate and Parnwell. A report to go before the CPCA transport committee on September 9 stated: “There would be no significant change to overall service levels [in Peterborough], but the network should be simpler to operate and explain.” The revised proposals were developed in response to a six-week public consultation that received 1,182 responses. Residents emphasised the need for reliability, punctuality, frequency, operating hours, access to rail and healthcare, the need for clear information, affordability and integrated ticketing, and the importance of services that were usable for work, education, healthcare, shopping and leisure. If approved at next week’s meeting, the changes could be introduced from February 2027, with further changes planned for August 2027. CPCA Mayor Paul Bristow said: “Thank you to everyone who took the time to share their views as part of our Bus Network Review. “Listening to residents is incredibly important, because you are the people who use these services and understand what works well and where improvements are needed.” Fenland – Services 46, 50, 56 and Tiger 7 would be redesigned to create a clearer local network, including improved March–Wisbech links, better weekend provision and revised connections through Chatteris. St Ives, Earith, Somersham and Ramsey –  The 301 would be improved to provide a simpler, more frequent core service, with Tiger 12 withdrawn alongside replacement links and implementation planning. St Neots, Godmanchester, the Hemingfords and St Ives – Service 65 would be revised to serve St Neots Rail Station and extend from the Offords to Godmanchester, the Hemingfords and St Ives. Cambridge and South Cambridgeshire – Services including 8, 26, 27, 27A, 27H, 75, T2, T4 and T5 would be revised to improve reliability, provide more regular Cambridge links and support evening, weekend and peak-time travel. East Cambridgeshire and Suffolk links –  Several existing low-frequency services around Haverhill and Newmarket would be replaced by simpler services, including new 119, 120 and 121 routes.

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Cambridgeshire ‘school streets’ could be enforced with cameras
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Cambridgeshire County Council is considering the use of cameras to enforce school streets. School streets restrict car movements at drop-off and pick-up times to reduce pollution and encourage walking and other active travel methods. Cambridgeshire County Council’s highways and transport committee was asked to approve a report detailing their approach to using cameras to enforce traffic rules. They were told that “initial planning work” has started on installing Automatic Number Plate Recognition (ANPR) cameras to enforce turning restrictions on roads such as Downing Street. Council officers also said they had started looking into using the cameras to enforce school streets, but these would need further assessment before being approved. Cllr Darren Green, of Romsey, said he was “very, very happy” that the council was considering this. The Green councillor said: “We know already that school streets can be very fragile and rely on a lot of volunteer work and best practice would be to back this all up with a camera system. “I hope going forward, once this is in place, that we can prioritise using cameras on school streets.” Cllr Alex Beckett, chair of the committee, stressed that volunteers would still be important regardless of if the cameras had been installed. The Liberal Democrat councillor said: “When the general public see that there are actually members of the community willing to stand up and man the school streets, and protect that school, it has a much better impact that having a no-name camera that feels a bit like it’s the state doing it, or the council doing it, when actually most school streets are really supported by the parents and those there. “I think wherever possible I would support the use of volunteers on school streets but I do know that is increasingly challenging in some places. “In some places unfortunately the level of harassment that is given to those school streets volunteers means the cameras might be a better approach.”

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Free blood pressure checks at Huntingdon surgery as part of national campaign
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Huntingdon residents are being offered free blood pressure checks at Priory Fields Surgery on September 8 as part of a national campaign to identify the potentially dangerous condition. Priory Fields Surgery in Huntingdon is supporting Know Your Numbers Week by offering a free, drop-in blood pressure session on Tuesday, September 8 from 12.30pm to 2pm. High blood pressure, which affects around 14.4 million adults in England, is often undiagnosed and can lead to serious health problems. Dr Chris Smith from Priory Fields Surgery said: "High blood pressure is often called a silent risk because it rarely comes with obvious symptoms or warning signs. "However, leaving it unchecked over time significantly increases your risk of experiencing a stroke or heart attack later in life, and it can also quietly damage your kidneys. "The good news is that checking your numbers is quick, simple and straightforward. "Taking a few moments to get it checked gives you a clear picture of where you stand, helping you protect your long-term health before any harm is done." An estimated 5.5 million people are living with undiagnosed high blood pressure in England. The surgery, located on Nursery Road, is also encouraging residents to register with a GP if they have not already done so. Registration is available online at prioryfieldssurgery.nhs.uk/practice-information/new-patients.

The studio was founded by Pilates instructor Rose Parker, who spent time living in Tampa, Florida, and was influenced by the popularity and community atmosphere of studios there. Ms Parker said: "Pilates is much more established in the US, and when I was living in Tampa I loved the quality of the studios there and the communities that grew around them. "I wanted to create that same feeling back home in St Neots and make Flow State somewhere people actually enjoy spending their time, rather than simply somewhere they come to exercise." After securing the Tebbutts Road premises, Ms Parker enlisted Sandell Group to design and deliver a 10-week interior transformation designed to put community at its heart. The 1,900 sq ft studio was completed just 10 weeks after Ms Parker signed the lease. She said: "When I first saw the finished studio, I genuinely couldn’t believe it was real. "It was exactly how I had imagined it, and it felt like everything had been thought of." The design includes inward-facing Pilates reformer machines to encourage interaction among class participants. Ms Parker said: "I’d love Flow State to help more people in St Neots discover movement they love and become a place where the community can get stronger, meet other people and, most importantly, find somewhere that feels happy and enjoyable." Nissar Khan, head of business development at Sandell Group, praised the collaborative process and the finished result. He said: "Seeing Rose’s reaction to the finished studio was fantastic for everyone involved in the project. "We’re really proud of what we have created together."

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Inquest into death of 'beloved' Cambs mother who died unexpectedly at home
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: An inquest has been held after a "beloved" mother from Cambridgeshire who "touched the lives of many" died unexpectedly at home. Gemma Connor, 40, a mental health practitioner from Peterborough, died at her home on October 12, 2024. A fundraising campaign for Gemma’s funeral costs raised more than £5,000. The GoFundMe page reads: "Gemma helped so many people through her work and touched the lives of many personally too. "She will be incredibly missed and we want to give her a lovely send off." Gemma’s daughter Jasmine told the Nottingham Post her mother’s death was a complete shock and that she “lit up every room”. The inquest into her death was formally concluded on September 3, at Vantage House in Huntingdon. Area Coroner for Cambridgeshire and Peterborough Caroline Jones expressed "sincere apologies" to Gemma's family for the amount of time taken to conclude proceedings. The inquest heard from Gemma's GP, Dr Deepali Prakash, that she had a history of health conditions including acute pancreatitis, fatty liver condition and alcohol dependency. She had also been prescribed several medications. The inquest heard from dieticians who Gemma had spoken to in early 2024, who said she was seeking advice on unintentional weight loss and nausea. She was advised to aim for a high energy, high protein diet and avoid too much fat. Gemma had been supported by a drug and alcohol service for alcohol dependency but asked for her file to be closed in April 2024. The inquest heard that on October 11, 2024, Gemma went to bed at her home in Peterborough at around 11.30pm. About half an hour later, her partner woke to find her unresponsive and breathing shallowly before calling 999. He was advised to begin CPR and the emergency services arrived soon after. Paramedics used a defibrillator and attempted resuscitation but Gemma was in cardiac arrest and they could not revive her fully. Her death was confirmed at around 2am on October 12, 2024. The post-mortem found no alcohol in Gemma’s blood but detected prescribed medication, including morphine. All the medication was within therapeutic levels except morphine, which was at a high, possibly toxic level. But Coroner Jones said the level could not be confirmed as toxic because this often depends on an individual’s tolerance. Gemma's cause of death was labelled as 1a respiratory failure due to morphine toxicity with contributing conditions of chronic pancreatitis and liver disease. Coroner Caroline Jones said this was not the same as an overdose because Gemma’s health conditions may have changed how her body absorbed the medication. In her closing statement, Ms Jones said: “I would like to extend my condolences to you all and Gemma's wider family and friends for your loss.”

Detective Constable Sarah Hurrell, who investigated the case, said: "Ashton’s ongoing campaign of harassment left the victim living in fear, and in a constant state of emotional distress. "Ashton was manipulative in his emails, and used emotionally abusive tactics to prey on the victim’s kindness, guilt-tripping her into thinking he would harm himself if she did not respond." On Friday, August 28, he was jailed for two years and eight months at Cambridge Crown Court after admitting stalking and breaching a non-molestation order. School Keep Clear signs have appeared on a road in Sawtry outside an empty field where a primary school has been planned for years, but is yet to be built. He demanded an explanation of why the markings were installed, who authorised the work and whether the bus stop would ever become operational. Meridian Trust will run the new school, which is intended to serve children from Sawtry's new housing developments. The school is expected to open initially to Reception applications only before expanding as its first intake moves through the years. The council says construction will be timed using pupil forecasts and ongoing monitoring of numbers in the area. The first phase is expected to be completed before the school is needed. The council, Department for Education and Meridian Trust will keep the opening date under review to meet community needs without undermining Sawtry's existing schools. He said: "For local residents who have waited patiently for this much-promised new school, I can completely understand why the irony of these markings has not gone unnoticed. "Perhaps the county council administration could apply the same urgency to actually delivering the school as it has to painting the road outside it." He called on the county council to issue a formal statement addressing residents' concerns. Mr Bywater also said MP Ben Obese-Jecty had been kept informed and had asked to be briefed as the situation developed. A Cambridgeshire County Council spokesperson said: “These school road markings have been installed prematurely in error by contractors working on behalf of the Glatton Road housing developer. “As a school is not yet operational at this location, we have asked the developer to remove these school markings as a priority and at their own expense.” The early years facility is planned to provide 52 places, subject to demand, while the school design includes roof-mounted solar panels, natural ventilation and reduced reliance on artificial lighting.

Mr Glover, who joined the board of trustees in March 2026, is a business leader with experience in the IT and telecommunications sectors. He said: "Caring Together is a meaningful charity with a very valid purpose, which is why I wanted to get involved. "The charity is in really good shape and that’s largely because of Stuart and Miriam’s leadership. "I’m looking forward to helping Caring Together build on these strong foundations as it strives to reach and support even more unpaid carers." Mr Glover also brings personal experience of caring, having helped look after his mother-in-law, who had Alzheimer’s. Ms Martin welcomed the new appointment. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Residents lead effort to tackle speeding and make roads safer
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Share Residents are taking the lead in making their roads safer by tackling speeding head-on. In Cambridgeshire, more than 1,000 volunteers are involved in the Community Speedwatch scheme, which aims to reduce speeding and promote safer driving through community action and support from the police. Central to the scheme’s success is Julie Clark, the force-wide Watch Coordination Officer, who has dedicated nearly two years to supporting volunteers, coordinating schemes, and addressing community concerns. Ms Clark said: "Being part of the Vision Zero initiative means so much. "To be given joint responsibility with my team to help reduce the number of people killed or seriously injured on Cambridgeshire's roads is a privilege. "I am so grateful to members of the community who volunteer their free time to help keep Cambridgeshire's roads safe." Community Speedwatch now operates in 113 groups across the county, with four additional HGV Watch schemes. Trained volunteers monitor vehicle speeds and gather data in areas where speeding is a concern. Their work contributes to educating drivers and providing valuable information to police and road safety partners. Police and Crime Commissioner Darryl Preston, who chairs the Cambridgeshire and Peterborough Vision Zero Partnership, said: "Every death or serious injury on our roads is one too many. "Community Speedwatch demonstrates what can be achieved when local people, volunteers, and partner organisations work together towards a common goal. "Julie’s passion and commitment, alongside the incredible dedication shown by our volunteers, is helping create safer roads across Cambridgeshire. "As chair of the Vision Zero board, I remain committed to investing in practical initiatives that educate drivers, reduce speeding, and ultimately save lives." The initiative is supported by the commissioner’s Vision Zero safety vans, which serve as a visible deterrent and reinforce the importance of driving safely. Parish councils, community groups, or residents interested in starting a scheme can contact Julie Clark at speedwatch@cambs.police.uk. Share

Crews from Dogsthorpe, Stanground, the north roaming fire engine, Whittlesey, Huntingdon, Thorney, St Neots, Ramsey and Sawston attended. The fire has now been burning for more than a week, but Cambridgeshire Fire and Rescue said that crews are expected to remain at the scene "for the foreseeable future". In a statement from today (August 17), the fire service said crews are still working to extinguish the fire. Wayne Swales, area commander at Cambridgeshire Fire and Rescue Service, said: "Although temperatures have reduced from during the week, it has still been hot on the fireground, but crews have stood up to the challenge exceptionally. The fire service said crews are still working to extinguish the fire (Image: Cambridgeshire Fire and Rescue) "Thanks to the fantastic teamwork from all crews across the county and the incredible support from our National Resilience colleagues from all over the country, we look to be a better position. "Steady progress has been made and we are discussing our tactics regularly to try and hopefully start to scale back our firefighting. "We will know more over the next day or so." Mr Swales said the service has been "overwhelmed" by support from the public and thanked everyone who has donated. He also praised partner agencies for their assistance, particularly Natural England.  The fire follows a recent Government emergency alert warning of increased wildfire risk on Friday (August 14). Residents are being urged to stay vigilant and help reduce the risk of further fires. The fire service has advised the public to dispose of cigarettes safely, take litter home, avoid barbecues and bonfires, and not use fireworks. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: St Neots traders praise council takeover but call for advertisement of market days
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Share Share Traders have urged Huntingdonshire District Council to better advertise market days as they fight to adapt to changing shopping trends. St Neots Market, held every Thursday in the Market Square, was taken over by Huntingdonshire District Council in November. It followed a multi-million-pound refurbishment of the square which was closed for over a year while works were carried out. Phil Anderson has been trading at St Neots for around 20 years, and said the market has improved since the council took it over. The 70-year-old said: “The improvements have been very good, footfall has increased dramatically which is surprising considering the town is losing its shops rapidly. It normally drops when the kids go on holiday but it hasn’t been too bad.” Richard McCann first set up on the market square about five months ago but before that was trading in other markets across the country. The 62-year-old said the market could be advertised better on social media. He said: “I think it does help – I do a pub car park in Bournemouth and I’m mobbed, they’re quite good on social media.” One trader, who did not want to be named, said that trade is tough but it’s “nothing to do with the council”. He said: “Shops and banks are closing – we bounce off the shops and they bounce off us. All the rates, national insurance, it’s ridiculous.” Emma, who did not give her surname, said that free parking could help to attract customers to the market square. She said: “There’s no free parking here at all – if they made the first hour free I think that would help.” Mathew Thornton was a trader at Huntingdon market when he was told a spot was available at St Neots and decided to give it a go. The 46-year-old said: “The weather is unbearable but the footfall is just the same for me.” Jimmy Singh has been trading at the market for 38 years and said he’s seen a “hell of a lot of change” with “not even a quarter” of traders left. The 72-year-old said: “We need more traders in the market – we have seven stalls and it’s not enough. It used to be in a big square like this, you would have more than 60 traders.” Read more Work begins on new £30 million Hunts sport and health hub New chair appointed to lead board of Cambs charity 10 road closures in Cambridgeshire you should be aware of this week Paul Firman, the market’s “longest serving green grocer”, said the council does what they can to help but markets everywhere are struggling. The 66-year-old said: “They don’t do a bad job but the market has changed since Covid – people’s shopping habits have changed. “What can be done – what can be done about the high street? They aren’t doing a bad job – the rent is reasonable and they look after you. It’s a shame the way things are going but it’s the same with pubs – this country is built on small businesses. When I first came here 38 years ago there were five green grocers and the market was absolutely buzzing, but so was every market.” He also said the council could advertise Thursday’s market better – like they do for the farmer’s market, held twice a month. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Man strangled and grabbed ex-partner by hair in 'violent' attack
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Share A man who followed and strangled his ex-partner in a violent attack has been jailed. Fred Lamb, 43, targeted the woman as she cycled past the Grafton Centre car park in Cambridge at around 6pm on February 23. He called out to her, but she ignored him and continued cycling. Lamb then followed her on his own bike, repeatedly shouting her name. He followed her into Discovery Way, where he deliberately crashed the front wheel of his bike into hers, causing her to fall. He then got on top of her and shouted: "Give me your money". The victim tried to escape, but Lamb grabbed her by the hair and searched her pockets. When she pushed him away, he bit her fingers. CCTV audio captured the victim telling him: "I'm not coming with you, let go of me. "Just go, just go." She was later heard saying: "Please, you're being nasty," before screaming: "He's biting me, help, help." The woman managed to break free and ran towards a nearby address. As she reached the front door, Lamb placed his hands around her neck and squeezed. Two members of the public intervened, shouting that they were calling the police. They told Lamb to leave the victim alone and he walked away from the scene. Officers arrived and found Lamb hiding in a bush on a nearby street, where he was arrested. At Peterborough Crown Court on Thursday, August 13, Lamb, of no fixed abode in the Cambridge area, was sentenced to one year and four months in prison. He after pleaded guilty to intentional strangulation. A charge of assault with intent to commit robbery was ordered to lie on file. Detective Constable Edward McAuley said: "This was a terrifying attack on a woman who was simply trying to go about her day. "Lamb repeatedly targeted the victim, assaulted her and then strangled her as she desperately tried to get away from him. "Strangulation is an extremely serious offence which can have devastating and long-lasting physical and psychological effects. "I would like to commend the victim for her bravery throughout the investigation and thank the members of the public who stepped in to help and contacted police. "I hope this sentence demonstrates that we will pursue offenders and do everything we can to protect victims from violence and abuse." Have you got a story you want to share? A temporary solar farm has been approved in the Cambridgeshire countryside despite fears it will harm the green belt. The development would also include a battery energy storage facility and developers Innova Renewables said it could power around 13,422 homes annually. They said the panels would deliver up to 49.99MW of renewable energy and 10MW could be stored. South Cambridgeshire District Council’s planning committee considered the application for a 40-year operational period, after which the site would be restored to agricultural use. Concerns had been raised about the 74 hectare site off Low Fen Drove Way in Horningsea’s impact on nearby Grade-II listed Biggin Abbey. The proposal is also next to a site where the sewage treatment works in Cambridge was set to be relocated – but the future of this is unclear after the government withdrew funding. The application was recommended for approval by council officers who said it would be “temporary and low scale” and considered the land to be grey belt – a site considered to make only a limited contribution to the green belt. John Hughes, from the National Trust, said that “significant opportunities” were missed in the application to improve biodiversity and nature recovery. He said: “With a close proximity to Cambridge and other local populations, an opportunity to better connect with people and nature has been missed along with the varied social benefits it would provide.” Although the scheme “substantially exceeds” the requirement for biodiversity net gain, Mr Hughes said this was largely through “passive measures” like the conversion of arable land to grassland. He said: “For a development of this scale on green belt land we would have expected a more ambitious and integrated approach to nature recovery.” An agent for the developer said the scheme had “significant benefits” and would support “both local and national renewable energy and decarbonisation targets”. She said: “South Cambridgeshire Council declared a climate emergency in 2019 and this year’s climate and nature strategy committed to a 50 per cent reduction by 2030 and net zero by 2050 for area wide emissions. “This is well evident in the climate conditions we’re seeing across the UK and Europe this week.” Councillor Anna Bradnam, speaking as ward councillor for Milton and Waterbeach, said that although the scheme is described as temporary, “40 years is half a lifetime”. The Liberal Democrat councillor said: “I respect the officer’s view but regret that the green belt protections which used to be so strong have been eroded by this concept of grey belt. “I believe this development would have a degrading and industrialising impact on the countryside in this area – how can 74 hectares of glass and metal for 40 years be considered a minor adverse impact?” Cllr Vivien Biggs, of Swavesey, said that the development couldn’t be argued to enhance the area, but they had to consider balance. The Liberal Democrat councillor said: “I think we have to be pragmatic, and obviously anybody having something like this in their back yard is not going to be particularly happy. “It’s not beautiful, but we also know we don’t own the view unless we own the land.” Cllr Heather Williams, of The Mordens, also said that planning was about “trade-offs” and there will never be a “perfect solution”. The Conservative councillor said: “There’s merit for it in its objectives but, in my view, there’s a lot of policies it comes into conflict with. “I think we need more renewable energy and I 100 per cent understand why farming communities are looking to things like solar in the current situation – but there are alternative places.” The solar farm was approved with four voting in favour and one against. Callum Liddle, 38, of no fixed abode but from the Peterborough area, flew into a rage after his partner received a text message from another man on July 19 last year. As she stood up from a chair, he blocked her exit, pushed her, and physically assaulted her. He grabbed her by the hair, pushed her into bookshelves, threw her to the floor, and kicked her in the back three times. Liddle pleaded guilty to intentional suffocation and assault occasioning actual bodily harm (ABH), as well as assault by beating relating to a separate incident involving another victim in May last year. He was sentenced to two years and seven months in prison at Peterborough Crown Court on August 7 and was given a ten-year restraining order. St Ives-based Dinky Little Dot Photography is celebrating 10 years of specialising in newborn and baby photography, offering families timeless portraits and lasting memories. Founded and run by Laura, the studio creates a calm, welcoming space for newborn, maternity, baby milestone, cake smash and family photography sessions in St Ives, Cambridgeshire. Laura said: "Photography has always been something I’ve loved, but after seeing just how quickly babies change during those first few weeks of life, I realised how important it is to preserve those memories. Laura said: "Supporting local businesses has such a positive impact on our community. Plans for a retirement home on land allocated for a pub in a town residents said “desperately” needs more places to meet have been refused. Central Cambourne had few pieces of land left undeveloped when the application was decided, with the area next to the Holiday Inn Express off Back Lane one of them. Permission for a restaurant and pub had been granted for the site, but it was still empty when the 58 retired living apartments were proposed. McCarthy Stone Retirement Lifestyles Limited claimed the scheme would provide “much needed” retirement accommodation in the area. But one resident, in a written objection submitted to South Cambridgeshire District Council, said there were “still many unsold McCarthy Stone retirement flats in their other Cambourne developments”. Another written objection said: “The last thing Cambourne needs is another retirement development. “There are thousands of people now living in the various Cambourne sections with more development being carried out. There is nowhere for people to go, nothing to do, and the one GP surgery is struggling; one pub, one coffee shop. “My view is that another retirement block will do nothing to enhance the town.” The council’s planning committee were asked to decide on the application, which they were recommended to refuse, on Wednesday (August 12). Julie Ayer, speaking on behalf of Cambourne Town Council, said the design of the development “simply doesn’t fit”. She said: “Cambourne is a vibrant, active community which embraces development and accepts and encourages change – but not at any cost. “Unfortunately, the application before you today is not one of a quality that Cambourne Town Council feel they can support for several reasons. “The design and form of this proposed development is poor and doesn’t enhance the character or have any social inclusion benefits within it.” Cllr Helene Leeming, speaking as a ward councillor for Cambourne, said the site was “one of the last unallocated parcels of land” in the town centre. The Liberal Democrat councillor said: “A town that desperately wants more places where people can meet and spend leisure time. “Earlier plans to build a pub there were supported, but a residential block like this removes the opportunity for this piece of land to be available to the community. “Cambourne needs more than just housing to thrive.” She said that 61 residents had written to object to the scheme, and said the design was “overcrowded, uninteresting and blocky”. Cllr Michael Booth, also of Cambourne, added that the development would be “fundamentally unsafe”. A new study by Cured Pharmacy has revealed that the Cambridgeshire and Peterborough Integrated Care Board (ICB) tops the national ranking for prescription spending, totalling £401,425,034 for a population of 1,056,872. This works out to £379.82 per person—the highest in the country. Despite not having the highest prescription volume, the cost per item is the most expensive in England at £17.12. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Cambridge South has halved journey times say NHS staff
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Share Share NHS staff said Cambridge’s newest station has already halved commutes while debate remains around its lack of parking. Cambridge South station is connected to the city’s cycle network and next to the guided busway system, with Trumpington Park and Ride (P&R) less than 20 minutes away. Though there isn’t any general parking for commuters – unlike the main station which has hundreds of spaces – there are five blue-badge bays for those with disabilities and space for pick-up and drop-offs. The station first opened its doors to passengers on June 28 with trains to London, Birmingham, and Stansted Airport. Kinga Bozek, who lives in Trumpington, said she likes the new station but there could be more regular bus connections to the park and ride. The 47-year-old said: “I would like more connections and buses later on because when you come back later there’s a bus every 30 minutes, and it’s a 30 minute walk. “There should be parking to be honest – or more buses to Trumpington Park and Ride if they want to go for that. “But it’s better to come here even if we have to walk, because it’s better than walking from the main station.” Sue Furnell said it’s her first time using the station but she’ll definitely be using it more often to get to Addenbrooke’s. The 65-year-old said: “I think it’s brilliant – I don’t drive so the lack of parking wouldn’t really get to me.” Erika Nacario works in Addenbrooke’s and said the station opening has halved her commute from Royston. The 32-year-old said: “It’s very convenient and it’s saved me a lot of time – obviously it can vary in terms of delays, but that’s also the case for the main station. “I don’t drive at all – the one that drives is my fiance, but he works in Papworth so it’s more convenient for him too, it’s horrible traffic from Royston.” Councillor Imogene Blackburn-Horgan, ward councillor for Queen Edith’s which includes Addenbrooke’s Hospital, said it is hoped the well-connected station will reduce “parking stress” and “associated anti-social behaviours”. The Lib Dem councillor said: “With a site that is well supported by train and bus connections it aims to mitigate these issues and support local residents with their wish for more active travel and less traffic. “Being disabled, I have been able to travel via the new Cambridge South Train Station as it is on my doorstep and have found it easy to use the disabled parking, taxi drop-off/pick-up for travelling home and bus connections to reach the city.” Cllr Olaf Hauk, ward councillor for Trumpington, said both Trumpington P&R and Babraham P&R are available for rail commuters, with free parking for up to 18 hours. He said the station was designed primarily for patients, visitors, and staff travelling to the Biomedical Campus and Addenbrooke’s Hospital. He said: “It was not intended to be a starting point for long-distance journeys, which is why it was built without a car park. “People travelling to destinations further afield can use other stations in and around Cambridge, or access Cambridge South by public transport, walking or cycling. “Those who need to drive can use nearby Park & Ride sites, such as Trumpington or Babraham.” He said residents in the nearby Clay Farm and Glebe Farm estates raised concerns about parking after the station’s opening, but their roads are still privately owned by the developer, Vistry, which is responsible for enforcing parking restrictions. Cllr Hauk said: “Motorists who park in breach of those restrictions risk receiving substantial penalty charges. “As local councillors, we will continue to work with Vistry and the councils to ensure that the parking arrangements are fair and effective for both residents and visitors. “At the same time, we remain strong advocates for improving public transport and sustainable travel across Cambridge.” Share

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Travelodge apologise over bedbug outbreak as blogger bitten '100 times'
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary:
Share Share Travelodge have apologised after a travel blogger was bitten 'more than 100 times' by bedbugs. Hannah Stephenson stayed at the Newmarket Road branch of Travelodge in Cambridge on July 26 after a day out with a friend. The 31-year-old said she woke up the following day feeling itchy before discovering her arms were covered in red spots. After investigating her bedding, Hannah said she spotted blood stains and black dots on her pillow before discovering bed bugs crawling in the bedding. Travelodge apologise over bedbug outbreak as blogger bitten '100 times' (Image: Kennedy News/@thecapetownblog) Horrified, Hannah counted 37 bites on her left hand, with more appearing across her arms, chest, back, face and legs throughout the day. Hannah reported the issue to reception but said she was simply told to contact customer services by email and was assured the hotel room wouldn't be let again that night. After calling 111, Hannah was advised to visit a pharmacy where she was given steroid cream and antihistamines to tackle the bites. Hannah posted photos of her bites online, in a video that racked up more than 76,000 views. Although the bites have begun to heal she said they remain visible and now look like chickenpox marks. Travelodge said instances of bed bugs are 'extremely rare' and that housekeeping colleagues are trained to inspect rooms and spot early signs during routine cleaning. The chain confirmed there were bedbugs present in Hannah's room and said they are retraining the housekeeping team at this hotel. Travelodge have apologised to Hannah for the 'distressing' incident and claim they have 'resolved the matter to her satisfaction'. Hannah, from Bassingbourn, Cambridgeshire, said: "I woke up feeling itchy and I started to have lumps forming on my arms. "When I got up, I saw spots of blood on the pillow and black dots. I looked closer and I actually saw a bug on the pillow. "I checked the bedding and they were more in the bedding. As the day went on more and more bites started to emerge. "I counted 37 on my left hand alone but they are too many to count, definitely more than 100, they're really itchy. "I was horrified and shocked. I didn't expect it from a Travelodge, I always thought they are pretty reliable. "I went down to the front desk to check out. I told them and the guy said they wouldn't let out the room again that night and told me to email customer services. "I got a response back saying they will do an investigation, which can last five to eight days. "By the end of the week I was frustrated. I hadn't heard anything and wasn't even offered a refund for my stay. "I wanted to give them a chance to sort it out and a week later I made the video. "I'd like an apology and some compensation because it has caused me a lot of distress. The swelling has gone down. Now it looks like I have chicken pox." Forced to cover the bite marks with foundation while attending her cousin's wedding on August 5, Hannah said she also had to change outfits and wear a dress with long sleeves. Hannah said: "I feel really embarrassed, it's summer so it's not easy to cover them up. I wear long sleeve tops to cover the worst of it. "I felt really embarrassed going to a wedding. They're on my hands, which are hard to cover up, I feel very self-conscious. People are going to think I'm dirty or something. "I don't usually wear foundation but I went to buy one to cover up for the wedding, I couldn't wear my original outfit which had no sleeves. "I was always worrying that someone was going to notice my hands. They have improved but they still look really bad. "People have been horrified, they've said I look like I have a disease. Everyone is saying how bad it looks. Shocked, Hannah said she didn't expect to get bitten at Travelodge after having travelled around the world without an issue. Hannah said: "I don't think I'll ever stay at a Travelodge again. "I want to avoid hotels as much as possible but I can't do that forever. I will always check reviews very closely before I stay anywhere. "Even after a week I am sitting here scratching now. I've travelled everywhere, Africa, South Asia, and I got it in my home town. "I use steroid cream twice a day and take scalding hot showers." A Travelodge spokesperson said: "We are deeply sorry for Ms Stephenson's experience and recognise how distressing an incident like this can be. "The safety of our customers is our priority and we maintain stringent, expert-led measures to prevent and manage pest issues, including training our housekeeping colleagues to be vigilant and to spot early signs wherever possible. "Bed bug activity affects the wider hospitality sector and is completely unrelated to hygiene or cleanliness standards. "In the rare instance that an issue is reported in one of our hotels, we immediately take affected and surrounding
  rooms out of service for inspection and treatment by independent pest control experts. "We have apologised directly to Ms Stephenson and resolved the matter to her satisfaction." Share

The fire has now been burning for a week straight, but Cambridgeshire Fire and Rescue said that crews are expected to remain at the scene "for the foreseeable future", as the fire is very complex and deep seated. National Resilience teams and partner agencies are supporting the response. Mr Warren said: "We are extremely grateful to everyone that is pitching in to help. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Inquest into death of missing man whose remains were found in Wisbech field
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Share Share An inquest into the death of a missing man whose bones were found in a field near Wisbech has concluded. The remains of Sergei Voitechovic, a 34-year-old who had been missing since 2018, were discovered on May 18, 2025, in a field off Lynn Road, Walton Highway, near Wisbech. An inquest into Mr Voitechovic's death was held at Norfolk Coroner’s Court on August 14. Mr Voitechovic was born on August 11, 1990, in Lithuania, and had no history of employment or usual address identified. He had resided in the UK from 2015 until 2017 with periods in and out of the United Kingdom thereafter. He is confirmed to have returned to the United Kingdom on July 11, 2018. The court heard that he had struggled with drug use and gambling, leading to the breakdown of his relationship with his former partner, Agatha Parausete, in 2018. After Mr Voitechovic went missing, his sister Anna reported him to Cambridgeshire Constabulary on October 13, 2018. Neighbours at the time believed he had returned to Lithuania. The court heard that the remains were found by a member of the public in a field known as Richardson Bambers, which had been regularly ploughed and cultivated between 2015 and 2024. The remains of 34-year-old Sergei Voitechovic were discovered in a field off Lynn Road in Walton Highway last year (Image: Chris Bishop) A wallet containing old photographs and a sock containing what appeared to be human bones were found at the scene. Post-mortem testing confirmed they belonged to Sergei Voitechovic. Detective Sergeant Melanie Reid told the court that police found no evidence of third-party involvement in Mr Voitechovic's death. The remains were identified through DNA testing. In her narrative conclusion, assistant coroner Maeve Sykes expressed her condolences to Mr Voitechovic's family and friends. She said it was clear that Sergei was a much-loved son and brother who had his own difficulties which he was trying to work through on his return to the UK on July 11, 2018, shortly after he became a missing person. Ms Sykes added she can only imagine the anguish this has caused her family over the number of years before his remains were identified. Due to the condition and incomplete nature of the remains, the medical cause of death was recorded as unascertained. Share

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanTitle: Remains of missing Wisbech man found through 'cult offering' discovery, inquest hears
summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Share Share The remains of a missing man from Wisbech were discovered by a member of the public who speculated she had stumbled upon a cult offering, an inquest heard. The bones of Sergei Voitechovic, a 34-year-old who had been missing since 2018, were discovered on May 18, 2025, in a field off Lynn Road, Walton Highway, near Wisbech. An inquest into Mr Voitechovic's death was held at Norfolk Coroner’s Court on August 14. The inquest heard that Debbie Garrett was walking to the bus stop from her home on March 1, 2024, when she spotted unusual items at the entrance to a field off Lynn Road. She initially dismissed them as fly-tipping, as the area is known for rubbish dumping, but soon realised one of the items appeared to be a diamond ring. Ms Garrett noticed some items at the entrance to a field just after the roundabout entrance to Lynn Road leading north to Walton Highway. She began to question whether she saw a diamond ring as she continued walking. She later found that the items included jewellery, food, and flowers, and decided to leave them undisturbed. After discussing the discovery with her gardener, Tony, the pair speculated that the items could be part of a cult offering. An inquest into Mr Voitechovic's death was held at Norfolk Coroner’s Court on August 14 (Image: Chris Bishop) They avoided touching or moving anything, and Ms Garrett continued to observe the site during her regular walks. She never saw anyone placing any items or any vehicles in the area, but occasionally heard a flute being played poorly in the middle of the night. In December 2024, Ms Garrett decided to photograph the items to show her aunt. Believing it would be bad luck to touch the offerings, she refrained from moving them and continued her observations. On May 17, 2025, her gardener Tony visited and asked if the offerings were still appearing. The two decided to inspect the site together, and entered the field to examine the items. Ms Garrett picked up a piece of jewellery before putting it down and Tony pointed out a large bone nearby, which they initially believed to be animal remains. As she was leaving, Ms Garrett noticed a sock and picked it up, discovering a wallet inside containing old photographs. Suspecting a possible connection to a body, she returned to the site the following day. She tipped out the contents of the sock and found bones she believed to be part of a human foot. Ms Garrett moved some of the items to make them easier to find and then returned home to call the police. She also researched the value of the jewellery, which she identified as being from H Samuel and each costing £100. Ms Garrett directed police to the site and subsequently found further bones, which she also handed over to officers. She recalled that about two-and-a-half years earlier, a man had been staying in the treeline between the field and Lynn Road. He was described as being of average build, around 5ft 8in tall, and English-speaking. No further offerings have appeared since police attended, but Tony received an image of similar offerings in a field in Tydd St Giles. Share

summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Share The family of a former University of Cambridge professor at the centre of a plagiarism row have spoken of their "shock" after his death. Jason Arday, 41, was found "unresponsive" at a property in Battersea, south London, on Friday (August 14). The father-of-two, who became the university's youngest black professor in 2023, was tragically pronounced dead a short while after. A spokesperson for the Metropolitan Police said officers were called by the London Ambulance Service at 3.12pm. It followed a report that a man had been found unresponsive inside a property on Daley Thompson Way, where Arday lived. A spokesperson for the force said: “Sadly, a 41-year-old man was pronounced dead at the scene. “His next-of-kin have been informed and are being supported by officers. “At this time his death is being treated as unexpected, but is not believed to be suspicious. "The case is being investigated by officers from the Met’s Central South Command Unit. A file will be prepared for the coroner." In a heartbreaking tribute, Arday's family said they are “in shock to have lost this amazing father, partner, brother, uncle and son”. They added he had been subjected to "sustained" abuse since he became the institution's youngest black professor in 2023. “The campaign of misinformation was too much for Jason, who was a gentle man and who always wanted to see the best in everyone," they said. "We are in shock to have lost this amazing father, partner, brother, uncle and son. “We won’t comment further at this point beyond asking the press to leave us alone now, and to stop the campaign of harassment which has been waged against Jason and his family for too long.” Cambridge University Vice-Chancellor Professor Deborah Prentice said she had been left "deeply saddened" by Arday's death. She added: "Our heartfelt sympathies go to Jason Arday’s family and friends at this incredibly difficult time.” The news of his passing comes just weeks after Arday was accused of plagiarising from other students for his PhD thesis. On August 5, he resigned as professor of sociology of education at the University of Cambridge. Last week, the university launched an investigation into Arday's appointment and tenure at the institution. Mayor for London Sadiq Khan said Arday's passing was "a tragedy", adding "it should be a wake up call for all of us" For help and support, call the Samaritans for free from a UK phone, completely anonymously, on 116 123 or go to samaritans.org. summary:https://www.huntspost.co.uk/news.cleanSummary: Share Share An investigation has been launched after a two-year-old stray dog was found with "suspected deliberate injuries" hidden beneath its matted fur. Peanut, a Shih Tzu-Lhasa Apso cross was found in Ross Street, Cambridge, on July 2, before he was taken to Woodgreen Pets Charity. When he arrived, concerns were immediately raised about his condition, especially his fur. Peanut's coat was so severely matter that one of his ears became attached to his neck, preventing him from turning his head properly. Woodgreen's veterinary team safely clipped and removed the layers of matted fur. However, they discovered concealed beneath his coat a series of vertical wounds running along his body from his back to his belly. Although the injuries were healing, the pattern and nature of the wounds led the veterinary team to suspect they had been deliberately inflicted. Following his treatment, Woodgreen carried out an investigation into his owner's history. Peanut was found with several unusual wounds believed to have been caused deliberately (Image: RSPCA) This included scanning Peanut's microchip, investigating his previous ownership history and sharing information with the RSPCA. Emma Lyons, veterinary surgeon at Woodgreen Pets Charity, said: "Peanut's condition was one of the worst cases of matting we've seen. "His fur had become so overgrown and tightly knotted that one of his ears was effectively attached to his neck, severely restricting his movement and undoubtedly causing him significant discomfort. "Once we removed the matted coat, we discovered several unusual wounds along one side of his body. "While we cannot say with certainty how they were caused, their appearance is highly concerning and not something we would typically expect to see as the result of an accident. "Our priority was to relieve Peanut's pain, begin treatment and ensure he received the care he so desperately needed." RSPCA animal rescue officer Maya Thakrar, who is investigating the circumstances surrounding Peanut's injuries, said: "The injuries found on Peanut are extremely unusual. Peanut has made remarkable progress during his time at Woodgreen (Image: RSPCA) "Although they were already healing by the time he arrived at Woodgreen, they would have caused him considerable pain. "We are working to establish exactly what happened to Peanut and are particularly keen to speak to anyone who recognises him or knows who cared for him before he was found. "Even the smallest piece of information could prove vital to our investigation." Microchip data suggest Peanut was rehomed approximately six months ago, and the RSPCA is keen to trace the person who took ownership of him at that time. Despite everything he has endured, Peanut has made remarkable progress during his time at Woodgreen. Martina Cohen, dogs team leader at Woodgreen Pets Charity said: "Peanut's resilience has amazed everyone who has cared for him. "Our team feels lucky to have had the chance to watch him grow in confidence during his time with us, and his cheeky personality and zest for life is shining through more and more each day. "It's heartbreaking to think about what he's been through, but thanks to the dedication of our veterinary and care teams, he now has the chance of the happy future every dog deserves." extractedItems.meetingTitle: Cambridgeshire County Council Highways & Transport Committee (28 July 2026)
extractedItems.content: Approved updated Highways Asset Management Strategy and winter readiness program. Priority gritting routes across Huntingdonshire and rural connector roads (including B1040) scheduled for pre-winter surface sealing.

extractedItems.title: County Council Children & Young People Committee: SEND Provision & School Transport Update
extractedItems.meetingTitle: Cambridgeshire County Council Children & Young People Committee (14 July 2026)
extractedItems.content: Reported strategic review of Special Educational Needs & Disabilities (SEND) funding allocation. Includes improvements to rural home-to-school transport routes across Huntingdonshire.

extractedItems.title: Parish Council Governance: Highway Contractor Penalties & Flaxon Walk Parking Bay
extractedItems.content: Confirmed that the disabled parking bay at Flaxon Walk was completed that day, ahead of the anticipated timescale. Reported that LGR will affect highway maintenance contractors. Advised that, from September, if highway repairs are carried out to an unsatisfactory standard, councillors should report them to him. New reporting arrangements will be introduced, and contractors may face financial penalties for poor-quality work. Confirmed he is happy to assist by reporting highway issues where necessary.

extractedItems.title: County Council Reports £60m SEND Budget Overspend
extractedItems.content: Reported that Cambridgeshire County Council is forecasting a £60 million overspend on Special Educational Needs and Disabilities (SEND), representing around 50% of the service's budget. Advised that, despite the significant overspend, there has not yet been any noticeable improvement in the service and encouraged councillors to report any specific SEND issues so that they can be raised. Cllr S. White suggested that it may be worthwhile contacting the local school to discuss any SEND-related concerns and gather further information.

extractedItems.title: HDC Local Plan Publication & Autumn Public Consultation
extractedItems.content: Advised that the Local Plan is due to be published in September and encouraged members to submit any comments during the consultation period.

extractedItems.content: Confirmed he will be looking into the future of Newman Stores, including speaking with the owner and liaising with the planning department to help move the matter forward.
